stories.title: The Legend of Queen Padmini
stories.story:
## The Legend of Queen Padmini — the mirror, the palanquins and the fire of Chittor

*The siege of Chittor by Alauddin Khalji in 1303 is recorded history; the story of Padmini first appears in Malik Muhammad Jayasi's poem Padmavat, written in 1540, and grew richer in the tellings of the bards of Mewar. Where history and legend part ways, this story says so.*

Long before any poet sang of her, the fort of **Chittor** already stood on its great ridge above the plains of Mewar. The hill rises sheer from the land around it, more than three miles long and narrow as a ship, ringed with walls and gates and full of temples, tanks and palaces. Tradition says the first fort was raised by **Chitrangada**, a chief of the Mori clan, and that **Bappa Rawal** of the Guhilas took it in the eighth century. By the end of the thirteenth century it had been the heart of Guhila power for generations, and the Rawal who held it in 1302 was **Ratnasimha**, remembered in song as Rawal Ratan Singh.

This much is history. Ratnasimha came to the throne around 1302, and his reign was short. In the north, the Delhi Sultanate had a new and restless master, **Alauddin Khalji**, who had seized the throne in 1296 and spent the following years conquering one Rajput stronghold after another. Ranthambhore had fallen to him in 1301 after a long siege, and its ruler Hammir Dev Chauhan had died fighting. Chittor, the most famous fortress of Rajasthan, lay directly in the path of his ambition.

Legend gives that ambition a face and a name. The poets say that Ratnasimha's queen was **Padmini**, a princess from the island of **Singhal**, the land we now call Sri Lanka. In Jayasi's telling, a talking parrot named Hiraman carried word of her beauty across the sea to Chittor, and the king set out disguised as a wandering yogi to win her. He crossed the ocean, endured trials of fire and sea, and at last brought her home as his bride. Her beauty, the bards say, was like the lotus from which she took her name: so radiant that the lamps of the palace seemed dim beside her.

At the court of Chittor there lived a learned Brahmin named **Raghav Chetan**. The legend says he was skilled in sorcery, and that he was caught using his arts in a way that dishonoured the king. Ratnasimha banished him from Mewar. Raghav Chetan left the fort burning with resentment, and he went where a man with a grievance could do the most harm. He went to Delhi.

"There is a woman in Chittor," he told the Sultan, the bards say, "beside whom every jewel in your treasury is only coloured glass." He spoke of her eyes, her grace and her voice until the Sultan could think of nothing else. Whether a living woman ever stood behind these words, no chronicle of the time can say. But in the story, from that moment on, the march to Chittor became the pursuit of Padmini.

The Sultan's army arrived beneath the ridge in **January 1303**. The great camp spread across the plain between the rivers **Gambhiri** and **Berach**, and the siege began. The Rajputs held the gates, and the walls were too high and the slopes too steep to be stormed. Weeks became months. In the legend, the Sultan grew impatient, and he sent a message up the hill: he would lift the siege if he could only see the famous queen with his own eyes.

The demand outraged the court. No Rajput queen showed her face to a stranger, still less to an enemy at the gates. The nobles wanted to refuse outright. But the bards say a compromise was found, one that would save the fort without breaking the honour of the household. The Sultan might come into the fort as a guest, and he might see Padmini, but only her reflection, glimpsed in a mirror.

The story of the mirror is the most remembered scene of the whole legend. The Sultan was received in the palace with courtesy. Padmini stood at the edge of a pool, or on the steps of a pavilion, and a mirror was set so that he could see her image in it. For one moment the reflection trembled in the glass. Then she was gone. The guides of Chittor still show visitors the water palace that bears her name and the room where the mirror is said to have hung, although the building that stands today is much later than the fourteenth century.

That single glance, the legend says, was the Sultan's undoing and Chittor's. He left the palace more determined than ever to possess her. Ratnasimha, faithful to the custom of hospitality, walked with his guest down through the gates to see him off. At the last gate, the Sultan's soldiers, hidden in readiness, seized the Rawal and carried him away to the camp. The message came back up the hill: the king would be returned when the queen was sent.

The fort fell into despair. Then, the bards say, Padmini herself made a plan. She called for two warriors of her household, the uncle and nephew **Gora** and **Badal**. Gora was a seasoned fighter, Badal hardly more than a boy. "Send word that I will come," she told them. "Tell the Sultan that a queen does not travel alone. My maids and companions will come with me, each in her own palanquin."

The Sultan agreed. On the appointed day a long procession wound down the slopes of Chittor: palanquin after palanquin, curtained and swaying on the shoulders of bearers. The tellers do not agree on how many there were. Jayasi speaks of sixteen hundred, and other versions give seven hundred, or fewer. Inside each sat not a maid but an armed warrior, and the bearers themselves were soldiers with swords hidden beneath their cloth.

When the procession reached the camp, the queen's party asked that she be allowed a last meeting with her husband. In the moment that the guards drew aside, the curtains were flung open and the warriors sprang out. The camp dissolved into confusion. Ratnasimha was cut free, put on a horse and carried back towards the fort, while Gora and his men turned to hold off the pursuit. Gora fell in that fight. Young Badal rode back up the hill to tell the queen that her husband was safe and that his uncle had died like a lion. The bards still sing the meeting of Badal with Gora's widow, who asked him only one thing: how her husband had fought.

The rescue saved the king, but not the fort. The legend says the Sultan returned to the siege in fury, and this time he did not leave. Here the tellings diverge again. In Jayasi's poem, Ratnasimha dies not at the hands of the Sultan but in single combat with **Devpal**, a neighbouring king who had insulted Padmini in her husband's absence. In the bardic tradition of Mewar, he dies defending the gates. All of them agree on what came next.

When the stores were exhausted and there was no hope of relief, the women of Chittor prepared for **jauhar**. The bards say that Padmini led them. A great pyre was built, and the women came to it in their bridal clothes and finest jewels, singing, carrying lamps and offerings. Tradition speaks of thousands, and some tellings give the number as sixteen thousand. When the fire had done its work, the men of Chittor put on saffron robes, smeared their foreheads with the ash, opened the gates and rode out to die. When the Sultan entered the fort, the legend says, he found only ashes where the queen had been.

What does history say? The fall of Chittor is certain. **Amir Khusrau**, the poet who accompanied the Sultan, recorded that the fort fell in **August 1303** after a siege of about seven months, that the Sultan gave it to his son **Khizr Khan**, and that it was renamed **Khizrabad**. Khusrau does not mention Padmini, nor does any other writer of the time. The tale of the queen and the mirror first appears in Jayasi's *Padmavat* more than two centuries later, written in Awadhi far away in the east, and Jayasi himself ends his poem by hinting that his story is an allegory of the soul. Later chroniclers, both Persian and Rajput, took up the story and told it as history, and so did the British writer James Tod in the nineteenth century.

Most historians therefore treat Padmini as a figure of legend rather than of record. But for the people of Mewar, the question has never been only about records. The story of Padmini gathered into one woman the courage of all the women of Chittor, across all the sieges the fort would suffer, and it became one of the most loved and most retold stories in India. Poets wrote it in Rajasthani, Hindi, Bengali and Persian. Pilgrims and travellers still stand on the steps of the palace by the water, and imagine a face reflected in a mirror for a single moment, seven centuries ago.

## Remembered for

- **The mirror.** The legend that the Sultan was allowed to see Padmini only as a reflection is the most famous scene of the tale, still shown to visitors at Chittor.
- **Gora and Badal.** The uncle and nephew who led the palanquin rescue of Rawal Ratnasimha are remembered as models of loyalty, and Gora's death in the fight is sung by the bards.
- **The jauhar.** Tradition says Padmini led the women of Chittor into the fire rather than be captured, making her the most famous symbol of Rajput honour.
- **A real siege behind the legend.** Alauddin Khalji besieged Chittor from January to August 1303, gave the fort to his son Khizr Khan and renamed it Khizrabad.
- **Padmavat.** Malik Muhammad Jayasi's poem of 1540 is the earliest surviving telling of the story, and historians regard it as legend rather than record.
- **A story retold for centuries.** The legend spread through Rajasthani, Hindi, Bengali and Persian literature and remains one of the best-known tales of India.

stories.title: The First Jauhar of Chittorgarh (1303)
stories.story:
## The First Jauhar of Chittorgarh (1303) — seven months on the ridge, and a fire that became a vow

*The siege of 1303 is described by Amir Khusrau, who rode with the Sultan's army, and by later Persian chroniclers; the jauhar and the last ride of the defenders are remembered above all through the traditions and bardic songs of Mewar. Where history and legend part ways, this story says so.*

In the winter of 1302, news travelled fast along the roads of Rajasthan, and almost all of it was bad. **Alauddin Khalji**, Sultan of Delhi since 1296, had built the strongest army northern India had seen in generations. He had beaten back the Mongols at the gates of Delhi, conquered Gujarat, and in 1301 taken the great fortress of **Ranthambhore**, where Hammir Dev Chauhan had died with his warriors and the women of the fort had gone into the fire. Every Rajput court knew that the Sultan would not stop there. The question was only where he would strike next.

The answer came on **28 January 1303**, the day, according to Khusrau, that the Sultan's army set out from Delhi for **Chittor**. It was the most famous fortress in Rajasthan, the seat of the Guhila rulers of Mewar, raised on a long ridge that rises sheer out of the plain. Its ruler was **Rawal Ratnasimha**, who had only recently come to the throne. With him in the fort were the nobles of Mewar, among them **Lakshmasimha**, the Rana of **Sisoda**, a chief of a junior branch of the same Guhila house, together with his sons.

The Sultan's host reached Chittor and spread its camp across the plain between the rivers **Gambhiri** and **Berach**. Khusrau tells us that the Sultan pitched his own pavilion on a small hill nearby, from which he could watch the walls. From that vantage, the problem was clear. The ridge of Chittor is more than three miles long, its flanks are cliffs, and its single approach climbs a winding road through a series of gates. No army could simply climb it. The fort would have to be worn down.

So began a siege that would last about seven months. The Sultan's engineers set up great stone-throwing machines, the mangonels that Persian writers called *manjaniq*, and battered the walls from below. There were no cannon; gunpowder artillery would not come to the sieges of Rajasthan for another two centuries. Instead, there were stones the size of men, hurled day and night, and arrows, and the slow, grinding pressure of an army that could wait. When the Sultan's troops tried to storm the slopes, they were thrown back.

Inside the walls, life went on under the shadow of the machines. The fort held tanks of water fed by springs and rain, granaries, temples and houses. Its defenders took turns on the battlements, and at night they watched the fires of the enemy camp spread like a second city across the plain. The bards describe the women of the fort cooking for the warriors, tending the wounded and keeping watch alongside them. In the tradition of Mewar, the queen of the fort was **Rani Padmini**, and her presence gives the siege its most famous legend, though no writer of the time mentions her.

The monsoon came in the summer. The rivers rose, the plain turned to mud, and the camp of the besiegers suffered as much as the fort. But the Sultan did not lift the siege. Inside Chittor the stores were running low. Months of siege meant months without harvest, without trade and without any hope of relief. There was no other Rajput power strong enough to march against the Sultan. The defenders knew it, and the Sultan knew that they knew it.

The traditions of Mewar tell what happened then in a single, famous story. The **Rana of Sisoda**, Lakshmasimha, is said to have dreamed that the goddess of the fort appeared to him, hungry, and demanded the blood of royal sons. One by one, the bards say, his sons took command of the defence, each for a few days, and each died at its head. Only one, **Ajaysimha**, was sent away at his father's command so that the line would not end. It is a legend, told in the later chronicles, but it holds a truth the bards wanted to keep: that Chittor was defended not by one king but by a whole house, generation after generation.

When there was nothing left to defend with, the leaders of the fort made the choice that Rajput tradition calls **saka**. The women would not wait to be taken captive. They would go into the fire. The men, freed of the fear for those they loved, would open the gates and ride out to die. It was the same choice that had been made at Ranthambhore only two years earlier.

Tradition tells the night of the **jauhar** in detail. A great pit was dug and filled with wood, ghee and incense. The women of Chittor bathed and dressed as if for a wedding, in red and gold, wearing all their jewels. They came in procession, singing the songs of their families and their gods, carrying lamps and coconuts and flowers. In the bardic telling, Padmini walked at their head. Their children walked beside them. They stepped into the flames together, and the fire rose higher than the walls, so that the soldiers in the Sultan's camp saw the glow and understood what it meant.

At dawn, the men of Chittor put on **saffron robes**, the colour of renunciation. Some rubbed the ash of the jauhar on their foreheads. They chewed tulsi leaves, said farewell to the fort, and threw open the gates. Then they rode down the slopes into the army below. None of them expected to return, and the bards say that none did.

The historical record of the end is harsher and less clear. Khusrau tells us that the fort fell on **26 August 1303**. He writes that the Rai of Chittor came out and submitted to the Sultan and was spared, while the Sultan, in his fury, ordered the killing of some **thirty thousand** people of the surrounding country. The tradition of Mewar remembers instead a ruler who died fighting at the gates. Historians still debate what became of Ratnasimha. What is not in doubt is that the victory was followed by slaughter, not mercy. The story that the Sultan was so moved by the courage of the dead that he ordered his soldiers to honour them is not found in any source of the time, and the writer who stood beside him tells us the opposite.

The Sultan gave the fort to his young son **Khizr Khan** and renamed it **Khizrabad**. Tradition credits the new masters with building the stone bridge over the Gambhiri, which still stands at the foot of the hill. But Delhi could not hold Chittor easily. Within a few years the fort was handed to **Maldeva**, a Songara Chauhan chief of Jalor who served the Sultan. And in the hills, the line that had been saved from the fire was growing up. **Hammir Singh**, the grandson of Lakshmasimha of Sisoda, would win Chittor back for Mewar some two decades later, and from him descend the **Sisodia** Maharanas who ruled Mewar until the twentieth century.

So the first saka of Chittor was not only an end. It was also the beginning of a new chapter in the history of Mewar. The house of Sisoda, which had given its sons to the defence of the fort, became the royal house of the kingdom. And the memory of that night became something more than a memory. It became a vow.

For centuries afterwards, when Chittor was threatened again, its people remembered 1303. The fort would see two more sakas, in 1535 and in 1568, and each time its defenders knew they were following a path already walked by their ancestors. The principle that the bards drew from the first jauhar, that honour was worth more than life, shaped the way the Rajputs of Mewar saw themselves for generations, for better and for worse.

Today, visitors to Chittor are shown the place where tradition says the jauhar fires burned, in the open ground near the **Samiddheshwar** temple and the **Gaumukh** spring. It is quiet there now, with pigeons on the old stones and the wind coming up over the edge of the ridge. Every year, the people of Chittor gather for the **Jauhar Mela**, a festival held in memory of the women of all three jauhars. They come with flowers and songs, and they speak the names of the queens who walked into the fire, as their grandparents did before them.

Seven hundred years have passed. The mangonels are gone, and so is the camp between the rivers. But the ridge of Chittor still rises out of the plain as it did when the Sultan first saw it, and the people who live in its shadow still tell the story of the first saka as if it were their own family's story. In a sense, it is.

## Remembered for

- **The siege of 1303.** Alauddin Khalji left Delhi on 28 January 1303 and took Chittor on 26 August after a siege of about seven months, as recorded by Amir Khusrau.
- **The first saka.** Tradition says the women of Chittor performed jauhar and the men rode out in saffron to die, the first of the three sakas of the fort.
- **The sons of Sisoda.** The bards tell that Lakshmasimha of Sisoda and his sons died defending the fort, while one son was sent away to carry on the line.
- **No mercy for the fallen.** Khusrau records that the Sultan ordered a massacre after the victory; the story that he honoured the dead has no basis in the sources.
- **Khizrabad.** The fort was given to Khizr Khan and renamed, before passing to Maldeva of Jalor.
- **The rise of the Sisodias.** Hammir Singh, of the house of Sisoda, recovered Chittor about two decades later and founded the line of Sisodia Maharanas.
- **The Jauhar Mela.** The women of Chittor's jauhars are still remembered every year at a festival held at the fort.

stories.title: The Second Jauhar (1535)
stories.story:
## The Second Jauhar (1535) — Rani Karnavati and the guns of Gujarat

*The second siege of Chittor is described in the Persian histories of Gujarat and of the Mughals and in the chronicles of Mewar; the story of the rakhi sent to Humayun comes from later tradition. Where history and legend part ways, this story says so.*

Two centuries after the first saka, Chittor had risen again, and higher than ever. The Sisodia house that won the fort back from Delhi in the fourteenth century had made Mewar one of the great powers of northern India. **Rana Kumbha** had ringed the kingdom with fortresses and raised the **Vijay Stambh**, the Tower of Victory, on the ridge of Chittor. His grandson **Rana Sanga** had fought the Sultans of Delhi, Gujarat and Malwa, and in 1527 he led a great confederacy of Rajput princes against **Babur** at **Khanwa**. That battle was lost. Sanga died in 1528, his body, the bards say, scarred by eighty wounds, and with him died much of the strength of Mewar.

The years after Sanga's death were bitter ones. His son **Ratan Singh II** reigned for only three years before he was killed in 1531 in a quarrel with the Hada chief of Bundi. The throne passed to his younger half-brother, **Vikramaditya**, still a boy. The new Rana was proud, quick-tempered and, the chronicles say, contemptuous of the great nobles of his court, who in return had little love for him. Real authority lay with his mother, **Rani Karnavati**, a princess of the Hada house of Bundi and one of Sanga's queens. She had two sons to protect: Vikramaditya, and a younger boy, **Udai Singh**.

Across the border to the south-west, in Gujarat, there ruled a Sultan who had every reason to strike. **Bahadur Shah** of Gujarat was ambitious and rich, and Mewar had long stood in the way of his house. He had absorbed the old Sultanate of Malwa in 1531, and Mewar, weakened and divided, now lay open before him. Above all, he had something the Rajputs of Mewar did not: a powerful train of **artillery**, served by gunners from the Ottoman world, led by an officer known as **Rumi Khan**.

Bahadur Shah first invaded in 1533. On that occasion, Karnavati chose diplomacy. She sent envoys, gave up lands in Malwa that Sanga had conquered, and paid a heavy price in treasure, including, the chronicles say, a jewelled belt that had once belonged to the Sultans of Malwa. The Sultan withdrew. But everyone knew it was a pause, not a peace.

He returned at the end of 1534, and early in 1535 his army surrounded Chittor. The scene beneath the ridge was very different from the camp of 1303. Now there were great bronze guns, dragged by teams of oxen, and the smoke of gunpowder hung over the plain. The walls that had defied the mangonels of Alauddin were now struck by iron and stone balls fired from cannon, and miners worked to dig galleries beneath the bastions and fill them with powder.

Inside the fort, Karnavati faced a crisis greater than the guns. The nobles of Mewar were unwilling to die for Vikramaditya, the young Rana who had insulted them. Many had stayed away. The tradition of Mewar tells that the queen mother summoned the chiefs and spoke to them not of her son but of Chittor itself. The fort, she reminded them, did not belong to one Rana. It was the fort of Bappa Rawal, of Hammir, of Kumbha and of Sanga, and the shame of losing it would fall on every house in Mewar. The nobles answered her call. They came back to defend the fort, though not for the boy who sat on its throne.

Two decisions followed, and both would shape the future. First, Karnavati sent her sons away. Vikramaditya and the small **Udai Singh** were taken secretly out of Chittor before the ring closed, and carried to safety in **Bundi**, the home of her own family, so that whatever happened to the fort, the line of Sanga would survive. Second, since the Rana himself would not be present, the defence needed a leader whom the nobles would follow. They chose **Rawat Bagh Singh** of Deolia, a senior chief of the Sisodia blood, who put on the royal insignia and took command in the name of the Rana.

There is one more story from these weeks, the most famous of all. Tradition says that Karnavati, desperate for help, sent a **rakhi**, the thread a sister ties on the wrist of a brother, to the Mughal emperor **Humayun**, asking him to come to her aid as a brother would. Humayun, the story goes, was moved, and set out with his army. But he came too slowly. Whether the rakhi was ever sent is uncertain: it does not appear in the writers of the time and is first told much later. What is known is that Humayun was at war with Bahadur Shah himself and was moving in his direction, and that, according to later Persian accounts, he chose not to strike while the Sultan was fighting the Rajputs. Whatever the reason, no help reached Chittor.

The guns did their work. A great mine was exploded beneath one section of the walls, and a breach was opened. The Gujarati army poured towards it, and the defenders threw themselves into the gap again and again. Among those who fell in the fighting at the breach, the chronicles of Mewar name chiefs from the leading houses of the kingdom, Hadas from Bundi, Rathores, Chauhans and Sisodias, fighting side by side for a fort that had united them in the face of ruin.

When it was clear that the end had come, Karnavati made the same choice that the women of Chittor had made two centuries before. Tradition says that she led the women of the fort into the **jauhar** fire, and gives their number as thirteen thousand. The bards describe it as they describe every jauhar of Chittor: the bridal red, the songs, the children walking with their mothers, the flames rising into the sky. It was the second time the ridge of Chittor had seen such a night, and it came after two centuries in which the fort had grown into a city of palaces, temples and towers. Everything that the Sisodias had built since the days of Hammir was now in the path of the fire.

The next morning, **8 March 1535**, Bagh Singh and the men of Chittor put on saffron and opened the gates. They died in the gateways and on the slopes, and the army of Gujarat entered the fort. Bahadur Shah had taken the most famous fortress of Rajasthan.

He did not keep it for long. Humayun now fell upon him, defeated his army near **Mandsaur**, and drove him in flight back into Gujarat. In the confusion, the Rajputs of Mewar returned to Chittor, and Vikramaditya was brought back from Bundi and set again on the throne of his ancestors. The fort that had been lost in March was in Rajput hands again within months.

But Mewar's troubles were not over. Vikramaditya had learned nothing from the disaster. His arrogance turned the nobles against him once more, and in 1536 he was murdered by **Banbir**, a son of Sanga's brother Prithviraj by a concubine, who seized the regency for himself. Banbir then went in search of the last of Sanga's sons, the boy Udai Singh. That night became one of the most famous stories of Mewar: the nurse **Panna Dai** placed her own son in the prince's bed, watched him killed in Udai Singh's place, and carried the true prince out of Chittor in a fruit basket.

Udai Singh grew up in hiding at **Kumbhalgarh**, won back his father's kingdom, and later, in 1559, founded the city of **Udaipur** beside the lake of Pichola. Nine years after that, Chittor would face its third and last great siege. The survival of the Mewar dynasty was in the end the work of three people: the queen who sent her sons to Bundi before the siege, the nurse who gave her own child for the prince, and the prince himself, who lived to build a new capital.

Rani Karnavati is remembered today as the queen who held Mewar together in its darkest years and chose the fire rather than captivity. The rakhi story, true or not, has made her name known far beyond Rajasthan, and every year, at Raksha Bandhan, it is told again across India. But in Chittor itself, she is remembered above all at the **Jauhar Mela**, alongside the women of 1303 and 1568, as one of the queens of the three sakas.

## Remembered for

- **Rani Karnavati.** The Hada queen of Rana Sanga and mother of Vikramaditya and Udai Singh, who held Mewar together after Sanga's death and led the jauhar of 1535.
- **The guns of Gujarat.** Bahadur Shah's artillery, led by Rumi Khan, battered and breached the walls of Chittor with cannon and mines.
- **The princes sent to Bundi.** Before the siege, Karnavati sent her two sons to safety at Bundi, preserving the line of Sanga.
- **Bagh Singh of Deolia.** The Sisodia chief who wore the royal insignia, led the defence and died in the last charge on 8 March 1535.
- **The rakhi to Humayun.** A famous tradition, uncertain as history, says Karnavati sent a rakhi to Humayun asking his help; no help arrived in time.
- **Chittor recovered.** After Humayun defeated Bahadur Shah near Mandsaur, the Rajputs retook the fort and Vikramaditya returned to the throne.
- **The road to Udaipur.** The young Udai Singh, saved again by Panna Dai in 1536, later founded Udaipur in 1559.

stories.title: The Third and Final Jauhar (1568)
stories.story:
## The Third and Final Jauhar (1568) — Jaimal, Patta and the last night of old Chittor

*The siege of 1567–68 is described in detail by Akbar's historian Abul Fazl in the Akbarnama and by other Mughal writers, and is remembered in Mewar through the chronicles and the songs of the bards. Where history and legend part ways, this story says so.*

By the autumn of 1567, the young Mughal emperor **Akbar** was twenty-five years old and master of most of northern India. One by one, the Rajput houses of Rajasthan had made their peace with him. The Kachwahas of Amber had joined him in 1562 and given him a daughter in marriage. Others had followed. But **Mewar** would not bow. Its ruler, **Maharana Udai Singh II**, the son of Rana Sanga and the boy whom Panna Dai had carried out of Chittor in a fruit basket, refused to attend the Mughal court or send his sons into Mughal service. He had also given shelter to Akbar's enemies. For Akbar, who meant to be the master of all Hindustan, Mewar was a challenge that could not be left unanswered.

In the autumn of 1567 the emperor marched. Tradition in Mewar tells that **Shakti Singh**, one of Udai Singh's sons, who had quarrelled with his father and was then in Akbar's camp, overheard the plan and rode home to warn him. Whether or not that is so, Udai Singh had time to prepare. His council of chiefs gave him advice that later generations would argue about for centuries. Chittor, they said, could not be held against the emperor forever, and if the Maharana was trapped inside, Mewar would lose its king along with its fort. Udai Singh should withdraw into the hills and carry on the war from there, while a garrison held Chittor as long as it could.

So Udai Singh left. Command of the fort was given to two men whose names would become inseparable. The first was **Jaimal Rathore**, a Mertiya Rathore chief of Merta who had himself lost his lands to the Mughals a few years before and come to Mewar to serve. The second was **Patta**, the young chief of **Kelwa**, of the Chundawat branch of the Sisodias. Under them, the chronicles say, were some eight thousand Rajput warriors, and with them thousands of peasants from the surrounding countryside who had taken refuge on the ridge.

Akbar arrived before Chittor in **late October 1567**. His camp stretched for miles across the plain, and he quickly surrounded the whole ridge, posting his commanders at every approach. He had brought what Alauddin and even Bahadur Shah had lacked: an organised Mughal artillery and an army that had learned siege warfare in years of campaigning. Yet the first weeks showed how hard Chittor would be. Assaults were thrown back from the slopes. The defenders' muskets and arrows took a steady toll, and the Mughal guns could not easily reach the walls high above.

Akbar turned to engineering. He ordered two great tools of siege warfare. The first were **mines**: tunnels dug beneath the walls and packed with powder. The second was the **sabat**, a covered approach, a long trench roofed with timber and raw hide, wide enough for horsemen to ride through side by side, which crept up the slope towards the walls so that the workers could advance under cover. The Mughal histories tell us that the men who built it died in great numbers every day under the fire from above, and that the emperor paid the labourers lavishly to keep them at work.

On **17 December 1567** the mines were fired. The first exploded and tore a breach in the wall. The Mughal soldiers rushed forward into the gap, and at that moment the second mine went off beneath them. Abul Fazl records that many of the emperor's men died in that explosion, among them well-known officers. The Rajputs rebuilt the breach that very night. It was a terrible day for the besiegers, and the defenders took heart.

But time was on Akbar's side. Week after week the sabat crept nearer, and the guns were dragged closer. By February 1568 the Mughal batteries were close enough to pound the walls directly, and the breaches grew wider than the defenders could repair. Every night Jaimal went along the walls himself, overseeing the work of filling the gaps with stones, timber and earth.

On the night of **22 February 1568**, Akbar was watching from the Mughal lines when he saw, by torchlight, a figure in the dress of a chief directing the repairs at a breach. The emperor was a fine marksman. He raised his own musket, which he called *Sangram*, and fired. The Mughal histories say the shot killed him; the traditions of Mewar say it struck him in the leg and crippled him. Only later did the Mughals learn that the man was Jaimal.

That night, the fires of **jauhar** were lit in Chittor for the third time. Abul Fazl writes that the Mughals saw fires burning at several places on the ridge, and that the Rajput nobles in the emperor's camp explained what they meant. Tradition says the jauhar was performed in three places, among them the houses of Patta and of other chiefs. The bards remember Patta's mother and his young wife, who, they say, put on armour and took up weapons and died fighting rather than enter the fire. Whether this is history or the gift of the bards, it is one of the most honoured memories in Mewar.

At dawn on **23 February 1568** the gates were opened. Tradition tells that Jaimal, unable to walk, was carried into the fight on the shoulders of his kinsman **Kalla Rathore**, a sword in each hand, so that the two men fought as one warrior with four arms. They fell near the **Bhairon Pol**, where cenotaphs to both stand today. Patta fell at the **Ram Pol**, the uppermost gate, where a memorial still marks the place. By midday the Mughal army was inside the fort.

What followed was the darkest hour of all. The peasants who had sheltered on the ridge and helped the defence were not spared. Abul Fazl himself records that the emperor ordered a general massacre, and that about **thirty thousand** people were killed. Many temples and buildings were damaged. The fort that had been the heart of Mewar for more than eight hundred years, since the days of Bappa Rawal, passed into Mughal hands.

Akbar was a man who knew the value of courage, even in an enemy. Later accounts say that he had stone statues of **Jaimal** and **Patta**, each seated on an elephant, set up at the gate of his fort. In the following century the French traveller **François Bernier** saw two such great stone elephants with riders at the gate of the fort in Delhi, and was told that they represented the two Rajput heroes of Chittor. The statues have not survived, but their story has.

The fall of Chittor changed Mewar forever. Udai Singh never returned to the fort. He devoted the rest of his life to the city of **Udaipur**, which he had founded in 1559, and it became the capital of Mewar. He died in 1572, and his son **Maharana Pratap** took up the struggle against the Mughals. Tradition says Pratap vowed not to sleep on a bed or eat from gold and silver plates until Chittor was free again, and that the Maharanas of Mewar kept a token of that vow for generations afterwards. Pratap never recovered Chittor. When his son **Amar Singh I** finally made peace with the emperor **Jahangir** in 1615, the fort was returned to Mewar, but on one condition: its walls were not to be repaired or fortified.

So Chittor became what it has been ever since, a fort of memory rather than a fort of war. Its gates, temples, towers and palaces still stand along the ridge, but it was never again the capital of a kingdom. The figure of thirty thousand dead, which some estimates count among the defenders and the people of the countryside together, made this the most terrible of the three sakas, and the last.

Today, the memorials of Jaimal, Kalla and Patta stand at the gates where they fell, and pilgrims touch them with reverence. Every year at the **Jauhar Mela** the people of Chittor remember the women of 1568 alongside those of 1303 and 1535. And in the songs of the bards, the names of Jaimal and Patta are almost always spoken together, as if they were one hero, the last defenders of old Chittor.

## Remembered for

- **The siege of 1567–68.** Akbar besieged Chittor from late October 1567 to 23 February 1568, using mines and a great covered approach called the sabat.
- **Jaimal and Patta.** Jaimal Rathore of Merta and Patta of Kelwa led the defence after Maharana Udai Singh II withdrew to the hills.
- **The shot in the night.** On 22 February 1568 Akbar shot Jaimal with his own musket as he directed repairs at a breach.
- **The third jauhar.** That night the women of Chittor performed jauhar for the third time, and at dawn the men rode out to their last battle.
- **Jaimal on Kalla's shoulders.** Tradition says the wounded Jaimal fought from the shoulders of Kalla Rathore; both fell near the Bhairon Pol.
- **The massacre.** Abul Fazl records that Akbar ordered a massacre after the victory, in which about thirty thousand people died.
- **The statues of the heroes.** Later accounts say Akbar set up statues of Jaimal and Patta on stone elephants at his fort gate.
- **The end of Chittor as capital.** Mewar's capital moved to Udaipur, and when the fort was returned in 1615 it was on condition that it not be refortified.

stories.title: The Miracle of Gaumukh Reservoir
stories.story:
## The Miracle of Gaumukh Reservoir — the spring that the people of Chittor call the gift of Ganga

*The story of how the Gaumukh spring was found is a local legend, told by the priests, guides and families of Chittor; the reservoir itself, the temples around it and the sieges it lived through belong to recorded history. Where history and legend part ways, this story says so.*

On the western edge of the great ridge of **Chittor**, where the land drops away in cliffs towards the plain, a flight of worn stone steps leads down into the rock. At the bottom lies a deep, still tank of green water, enclosed by walls and shaded by the cliff. Into it, from a stone spout carved in the shape of a **cow's mouth**, a thin stream of water falls without pause, day and night, summer and winter. This is **Gaumukh Kund**, the reservoir of the cow's mouth, and the people of Chittor have a story about how it came to be.

The legend begins in a time of drought. No one can say which year, or which king ruled from the ridge. The tellers say only that it was long ago, before the great sieges, when the fort was already old. For two years the rains had failed. The tanks of Chittor, which caught the monsoon water and held it through the dry months, had shrunk to cracked mud. The wells on the plain gave nothing but sand. Cattle died on the slopes, and the people of the fort began to talk of leaving the ridge altogether.

Among them, the story goes, lived an old holy man who kept a small shrine near the edge of the cliff. He had seen famines before. But this time he saw the children of the fort grow thin and the old people lie down and not rise, and he could not bear it. One evening he climbed down to the edge of the rock, where the ridge falls away towards the setting sun, and sat there without food or water. He would not move, he said, until the goddess of the rivers answered him.

"Mother Ganga," he prayed, "you came down from heaven to save the sons of Sagara. You flow through the hair of Shiva. Will you let the people of Shiva's own servants die of thirst on this rock?"

For three days and three nights he sat on the stone. The people of the fort came to watch him, and some thought he had gone mad with the heat. On the third night, the tellers say, he fell into a sleep that was not quite sleep, and a woman appeared before him, dressed in white, with a pot of water on her hip and a crown of lotuses. She did not speak. She only pointed down, to a place in the cliff face below where he sat, where the rock was cracked and a little moss grew in the crevice.

When the holy man woke, it was dawn. He called the men of the fort and told them to dig where the goddess had pointed. They thought it foolish, for there was no water on that dry cliff, but they had nothing else to try. They cut into the rock with chisels and hammers, and before the sun was high, the stone grew dark and damp beneath their tools. Then, the legend says, with a sound like a breath released, clear water burst from the cliff and ran down the face of the rock.

The people wept, and they named the spring **Gaumukh**, after the cow's mouth, because the water came from the rock the way the river Ganga is said to pour from the glacier at **Gaumukh** in the Himalaya, its sacred source. They believed that a thread of the holy river itself had come to Chittor. In time, the spring was given a mouth carved in stone in the shape of a cow's head, and the water was led through it into a great tank cut into the rock below.

That is the legend. What can be seen today is the work of human hands as well as of nature. The water that feeds the Gaumukh is a natural spring seeping out of the rock of the ridge, and the cow's mouth through which it flows is a carved stone spout, not a shape made by nature. The tank was cut and walled by the builders of the fort. Above it stands the temple of **Samiddheshwar**, a temple of Shiva that tradition links to the Paramara king Bhoja in the eleventh century and that was rebuilt by **Rana Mokal** of Mewar in the fifteenth. Close by rises the **Vijay Stambh**, the Tower of Victory, built by **Rana Kumbha** in the middle of the fifteenth century. The Gaumukh lies in the heart of the sacred ground of the fort.

There is good reason why the people of Chittor treasured it. A fortress on a high ridge lives or dies by its water. Chittor's builders knew this, and the ridge was once covered with tanks, wells and step-wells, gathering every drop of the monsoon rain. Tradition says there were once eighty-four of them; many still remain. In every siege that the fort faced, water was as precious as courage, and the springs and tanks within the walls were what allowed the defenders to hold out month after month. A spring that flowed even in the dry season was beyond price, and the people believed it was a blessing.

So the legend grew. People said that the water of the Gaumukh had healing powers, that a sick child bathed in it would recover, and that it had never once run dry, even in the worst years of drought. They said that as long as the Gaumukh flowed, Chittor would never truly fall. History gave that belief a hard test. The fort was taken three times, in 1303, in 1535 and in 1568, and each time its people paid a terrible price. But the believers have an answer: the walls fell, they say, but Chittor did not die. Its people returned, its temples were worshipped again, and the spring never stopped flowing.

The Gaumukh is also bound up with the memory of the queens of Chittor. Local tradition says that **Rani Padmini**, whose story the bards tell of the siege of 1303, came down these steps each morning to bathe and to pray at the shrine of Shiva above. Guides at the fort still tell visitors this, and point out the path she is said to have taken. The Padmini of the legend is a figure of poetry rather than of record, but it is easy to understand why the people of Chittor placed her here, at the most sacred water of the fort. And the open ground near the Gaumukh and the Samiddheshwar temple is where tradition says the fires of **jauhar** were lit. The spring of life and the place of sacrifice lie side by side.

Visitors who come to the Gaumukh today find it much as the pilgrims of past centuries did. The steps are steep and smooth from countless feet. The water in the tank is cool and deep, and full of fish, which visitors feed with handfuls of grain. Pilgrims take a little of the water in their palms and touch it to their foreheads. Some fill small bottles to carry home to those who could not come. The thin stream falls from the stone cow's mouth into the tank with a soft, unending sound, and in the heat of a Rajasthan afternoon the place feels like a hidden world, cool and green, beneath the dry, bright ridge above.

The holy man of the legend has no name in the story, and no tomb to visit. Perhaps he never lived at all. But the people of Chittor do not forget him. They say that when the water falls from the cow's mouth, it is still answering his prayer. And whatever the truth of the story, it holds something that every family on that ridge knew well, through every drought and every siege: that the water flowing out of the rock was a gift, and that a fortress, however strong its walls, was only as strong as the spring at its heart.

## Remembered for

- **The legend of the drought.** Local tradition says an old holy man prayed for three days to the goddess Ganga, who showed him in a vision where to find water in the cliff.
- **The cow's mouth.** The spring flows through a carved stone spout shaped like a cow's head, named after Gaumukh, the sacred source of the Ganga in the Himalaya.
- **The lifeline of the fort.** Springs and tanks like the Gaumukh allowed Chittor to hold out through long sieges, and tradition says the fort once had eighty-four water bodies.
- **Sacred ground.** The reservoir lies beside the Samiddheshwar temple and near the Vijay Stambh, at the heart of the fort's holy places.
- **A belief that outlived the sieges.** People say that as long as the Gaumukh flows, Chittor will never truly fall, and that its water heals.
- **Padmini and the jauhar ground.** Tradition says Rani Padmini prayed here every morning, and the jauhar fires are remembered as burning nearby.

stories.title: The Curse of the Fort
stories.story:
## The Curse of the Fort — a sage's words and the three fires of Chittor

*The curse of Chittor is a folk legend, told in many versions by the people who live around the fort; no chronicle records it. The three sieges it is said to have foretold are recorded history. Where history and legend part ways, this story says so.*

Every old fortress gathers stories the way its walls gather moss, and **Chittor** has more than most. It is the largest fort in Rajasthan, a walled ridge more than three miles long, and for over eight hundred years it was the heart of Mewar. It was here, the bards say, that Bappa Rawal made his capital, here that Kumbha raised his Tower of Victory, here that Mira Bai sang to Krishna. And it was here that three times the women of the fort went into the fire and the men rode out in saffron to die. When so much sorrow falls on one place, people look for a reason. In the villages around Chittor, many find it in an old curse.

The legend has no date. Some tellers place it in the earliest days of the fort, others in a time "when the kings had grown proud". They do not give the king a name, and that is wise, for the story is not history. But they all tell it in much the same way.

Once, they say, a ruler of Chittor sat in his hall of audience, surrounded by his nobles, his treasure and his guards. His armies had won every war. His walls were the strongest in the land. Poets praised him from morning to evening, and he had come to believe every word. One day a sage came up the long road to the fort, an old man in ash and rags, with a staff in his hand and the dust of many years of wandering on his feet. He had come, the story goes, to ask nothing for himself, only to warn the king of the suffering of his people in a year of scarcity.

The guards would not let him pass. When at last he reached the hall, the king did not rise. He did not offer water or a seat. He looked down at the old man from his throne and laughed.

"What can a beggar teach the lord of Chittor?" he said. "Look at these walls. No army on earth can climb them. Look at my treasury. No famine can empty it. Go and beg somewhere else."

The sage stood silent for a long moment. Then he struck his staff on the stone floor, and the tellers say that the lamps in the hall flickered as if a wind had passed through.

"You trust in your walls," he said. "Then let your walls be tested. Three times this fort will fall. Three times your people will pay for it, not with gold but with their lives. The women of this fort will walk into the fire, and the men will ride out to die. Your pride will be paid for in ashes."

The king's nobles drew their swords, but the sage was already walking away down the road, and no one dared to follow him. Some versions say the king repented and ran after him, begging forgiveness, and that the sage, moved, softened his words but could not take them back. "The curse will hold," he said, "until a day comes when this fort is no longer needed for war, and peace has come to the land around it."

That is the legend. The history of the fort, as it is recorded, is this. In **1303**, after a siege of about seven months, Chittor fell to **Alauddin Khalji**, Sultan of Delhi, and tradition remembers the first jauhar. In **1535**, it fell to **Bahadur Shah** of Gujarat, and **Rani Karnavati** led the women of the fort into the second jauhar. In **1568**, it fell to the Mughal emperor **Akbar**, after the defence led by **Jaimal Rathore** and **Patta** of Kelwa, and the third jauhar was performed on the night before the last battle. Three falls, three fires: it is easy to see how, looking back, the people of Mewar came to believe that the sage's words had come true.

It is worth saying plainly that the curse is a story told after the events, not a prophecy that anyone wrote down before them. The causes of the three sieges were the ambitions of sultans and emperors, the strength and weakness of the kingdom of Mewar, and the changing weapons of war, from stone-throwing machines to cannon and mines. But folk memory does not deal in causes. It deals in meaning. The story of the curse turned three separate disasters into a single tale with a moral at its heart: that pride brings ruin, and that the powerful must listen to the voice of the poor and the holy.

There is another curse that belongs to Chittor, and this one has a firmer place in tradition. After the fall of 1568, it is said, the Mughal victors gathered the sacred threads worn by the Rajput warriors who had died in the fort, and weighed them. The weight came to **seventy-four and a half** *man*, the old Indian measure of weight. In Rajasthan, the number **74½** became a curse. For generations, people wrote it on the outside of letters and sealed papers, and its meaning was understood by all: may the sin of the slaughter of Chittor fall on anyone who opens this unlawfully. Whatever the truth of the weighing, the custom shows how deeply the fall of Chittor marked the memory of the land.

After 1568, Chittor was never again the capital of Mewar. When the Mughal emperor **Jahangir** returned the fort to **Maharana Amar Singh I** in **1615**, it was on condition that its walls should not be repaired or strengthened. In a strange way, this fulfilled the last words of the legend. Chittor became a fort that was no longer needed for war. And so, the people who believe in the curse say, the curse ended there, and peace came to the ridge.

But not everyone agrees that the old fort is quiet. Many villagers and some visitors say that the spirits of the fallen still keep watch over Chittor. They say that on certain nights, especially on the nights of festivals and on dark moonless nights, sounds can be heard on the ridge that have no living source: the clash of steel, the neighing of horses, the beat of a war drum, and from the old palace grounds, faint and far away, the singing of women. Watchmen tell of footsteps on the ramparts when no one is there, and of lights moving among the ruins of the palaces near the jauhar ground.

These are the stories people tell, and they belong to the folklore of the fort, not to its history. No record and no historian confirms them. But they are told with deep feeling, and they are not meant to frighten. In the minds of those who tell them, the spirits of Chittor are guardians, not ghosts to be feared. They are the warriors who died at the gates, and the women who chose the fire, still keeping faith with the fort they loved. Some believe that they have protected Chittor from harm in the centuries since its last siege.

Today Chittor is a place of pilgrimage and of history. It is protected as a monument, and since 2013 it has been one of the **Hill Forts of Rajasthan** listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Historians come to study its temples and towers. Pilgrims come to the shrines of **Kalika Mata**, of **Samiddheshwar**, and of Mira Bai. Every year the **Jauhar Mela** brings thousands to remember the women of the three sakas. And in the evenings, when the light goes golden on the walls and the visitors have gone down the hill, the old men of the villages around the fort still sit together and tell the tale of the proud king, the sage with the staff, and the words that, they say, came true three times.

Is the story true? Almost certainly not as history. But it holds a truth of another kind. Chittor suffered more than any other fort in Rajasthan, and its people needed a way to understand that suffering. The legend of the curse gave them one. And its ending, in which peace finally comes to the fort when it is no longer needed for war, is perhaps the gentlest wish that the people of Chittor could make for the place where their ancestors died.

## Remembered for

- **The proud king and the sage.** Folk legend tells of a ruler of Chittor who mocked a wandering sage and was cursed for his pride.
- **Three falls foretold.** The curse is said to have foretold the three sieges and jauhars of 1303, 1535 and 1568, though the legend was told after the events, not before.
- **The end of the curse.** Tradition says the curse would end when the fort was no longer needed for war; after 1615 Chittor was never refortified.
- **The sign of 74½.** Tradition says the sacred threads of the warriors who died in 1568 weighed seventy-four and a half man, and the number became a curse written on sealed letters.
- **Guardian spirits.** Local people say the spirits of the fallen still guard the fort, and tell of sounds of battle and singing on certain nights.
- **A fort of memory.** Chittor is now a World Heritage Site and a place of pilgrimage, where the three sakas are remembered every year at the Jauhar Mela.

stories.title: The Underground Tunnels
stories.story:
## The Underground Tunnels — the hidden passages beneath Chittor

*The tunnels of Chittor live mostly in local legend and in the stories told by guides at the fort; a few cellars and passages can be seen, but no survey has confirmed the great network the legends describe. Where history and legend part ways, this story says so.*

Stand among the ruins of the palace of **Rana Kumbha** at Chittor in the late afternoon, and a guide will almost certainly lead you to a dark opening in the ground. Steps go down into shadow. The air that rises from below is cool and smells of stone and age. "This way," the guide will say, lowering his voice a little, "goes the tunnel." And then he will begin a story that the people of Chittor have told for generations: the story of the secret passages beneath the fort.

Chittor is the kind of place that invites such stories. The fort covers a ridge more than three miles long, and over eight centuries it was built over again and again by the rulers of Mewar. Palaces rose on the ruins of older palaces, temples on the sites of older temples. The rock of the ridge is full of natural cracks and hollows, and the builders cut cellars, cisterns, storerooms and water channels into it. When so much lies hidden beneath the surface, it is natural for people to imagine that even more lies further down.

The palace where the guides begin the story is itself one of the oldest and grandest buildings on the ridge. It takes its name from **Rana Kumbha**, who ruled Mewar from 1433 to 1468 and was the greatest builder in its history. He raised dozens of fortresses across the kingdom, among them **Kumbhalgarh**, and on the ridge of Chittor he built the **Vijay Stambh**, the Tower of Victory, to celebrate his wars against the Sultan of Malwa. His palace at Chittor, built on the remains of an older royal residence, was a maze of courtyards, halls, stables, zenana quarters and stairways. Today it stands roofless, its walls the colour of dust and honey, but it is still easy to imagine it full of life, and easy to understand why people believe its stones hide more than they show.

The legends say that beneath Chittor there runs a whole hidden world: a network of tunnels connecting the palaces to the temples, the temples to the tanks, and the heart of the fort to places far beyond its walls. In the stories they served many purposes. Kings and queens could pass through them unseen from one palace to another. Spies could slip in and out. Treasure could be stored in hidden chambers, safe from any thief or invader. And above all, when the fort was besieged, the defenders could use them to move men and supplies without the enemy below ever knowing.

The most famous of these legendary passages, the tellers say, runs from the **palace of Rana Kumbha** to the **Gaumukh** spring on the western edge of the ridge. In a long siege, they say, when every path in the open was watched and every water-carrier was a target for the enemy's archers and gunners, the women of the palace could go down into the dark and come back with water from the holy spring, and no one outside would know. Some say the passage ran on further, to the ground near the Samiddheshwar temple where tradition says the jauhar fires burned.

Another story tells of a great tunnel that ran from the fort under the plain for miles, coming out in a hidden place in the countryside. Through it, the legend says, a young prince of Mewar escaped from Chittor when the fort was in danger. In the version most often told, the prince was **Udai Singh**, and he escaped through the tunnel during the last siege of the fort.

Here history must correct the legend, because the real story is quite different and no less dramatic. Udai Singh was the son of **Rana Sanga**, and twice in his childhood he was saved from Chittor. Before the siege of **1535**, his mother **Rani Karnavati** sent him and his brother secretly to **Bundi** for safety. Then in **1536**, when the usurper **Banbir** murdered his brother and came looking for him in the night, his nurse **Panna Dai** put her own son in the prince's bed and carried Udai Singh out of the fort hidden in a basket, covered with leaves. The tradition of Mewar places that night in the very palace of Kumbha where the guides show the tunnel today. And when the last siege came in **1567**, Udai Singh, by then Maharana, was not in the fort at all. On the advice of his chiefs he had withdrawn into the hills before the Mughal army arrived, leaving the defence to **Jaimal Rathore** and **Patta**. He needed no tunnel.

So the tunnel of the prince is a legend. But it is easy to see where it came from. A prince really was carried out of Chittor in secret, in the dark, through the very palace where the opening now lies. Over time, the people of Chittor may have joined the true story of Panna Dai's courage to the mystery of the dark steps beneath the palace, and so the tunnel was born.

The story of the women and the jauhar has also attached itself to these passages. Guides at Kumbha's palace often say that the underground chambers below were where **Rani Padmini** and the women of the fort went into the fire in 1303. The story is told with deep feeling, and many visitors go down the steps in silence. But it is a local tradition, not a recorded fact. The palace that stands today was built largely in the fifteenth century, long after 1303, and the jauhar is more often remembered in the open ground near the Gaumukh and the Samiddheshwar temple. The Padmini of the legend is herself a figure of poetry rather than of record.

What can actually be seen? At Kumbha's palace and elsewhere on the ridge there are cellars, vaulted storerooms, cisterns and short passages cut into the rock. Some of them are blocked, some have collapsed, and some are closed to visitors for their own safety. Like any great fortress, Chittor certainly had storerooms, water channels and hidden ways of moving within its walls; in a long siege, stores, water and protected movement meant survival. But no archaeological survey has revealed the vast network of the legends, and no tunnel running for miles under the plain has ever been found. The passages that do exist are short and modest. The rest lies in the imagination of those who tell the story.

And the stories keep growing. Some say that the tunnels hold the lost treasure of the Ranas of Mewar, hidden before one of the sieges and never recovered. Some say that the passages are haunted, and that those who go too deep hear voices, or see a lamp moving far ahead in the darkness. Some say that the entrances were sealed long ago by order of the rulers, so that no enemy could ever use them, and that the secret of their routes died with the last men who knew it. None of this can be proved, and none of it should be taken as history. But it is part of the life of the fort.

Why do such stories last so long? Perhaps because Chittor itself is a place of hidden things. So much of its history was lost in the sieges and the fires. So many of the people who lived there left no names. The dark steps under the palace of Kumbha are a reminder that the fort we see is only part of the fort that was, and that beneath the ruins lie centuries of lives we can only imagine.

When the guide brings his visitors back up the steps into the sunlight, he will usually end the story the same way. "No one knows how far they go," he will say, and smile. "Some things Chittor keeps to itself." It is the right way to end. The tunnels of Chittor may be mostly legend, but the mystery they hold is real, and it is part of what makes the old fort so hard to forget.

## Remembered for

- **The tunnel of Kumbha's palace.** Guides at the palace of Rana Kumbha show an underground opening that local legend says leads to a hidden network of passages.
- **The secret way to the water.** Legend tells of a tunnel from the palace to the Gaumukh spring, used to bring water in secret during sieges.
- **The prince's escape, corrected.** Udai Singh did not escape through a tunnel: he was sent to Bundi before the siege of 1535, carried out by Panna Dai in a basket in 1536, and had left Chittor before the siege of 1567.
- **The jauhar tradition.** Guides say the underground chambers were the site of Padmini's jauhar, a local tradition rather than recorded fact.
- **What can be seen.** Cellars, cisterns, storerooms and short passages survive, but no survey has confirmed the miles-long network of the legends.
- **Treasure and ghosts.** Local stories speak of lost treasure, sealed entrances and lamps moving in the dark, part of the folklore of the fort.
