stories.title: The Construction Miracle of Sheesh Mahal
stories.story:
## The Construction Miracle of Sheesh Mahal — a thousand stars from a single flame

*The story of the architect's dream is a legend told at Amber by guides and craftsmen; the building of the palace by the Kachwaha rulers, and the making of the Sheesh Mahal in the seventeenth century, belong to recorded history. Where history and legend part ways, this story says so.*

On a rocky ridge above the lake of **Maota**, a few miles north of the city of Jaipur, the palace of **Amber** rises in tiers of honey-coloured stone and white marble. For centuries this was the seat of the **Kachwaha** Rajputs. Tradition says that the Kachwahas won Amber from the Meena chiefs who once held these hills, and that it remained their capital until 1727, when **Sawai Jai Singh II** founded Jaipur on the plain below. Above the palace, on a higher hill, stands the fortress of **Jaigarh**, and the walls that join the two climb and dip over the ridges like the back of a great sleeping animal.

The rise of Amber to greatness began in the sixteenth century. In 1562 **Raja Bharmal** of Amber became the first great Rajput ruler to ally himself with the young Mughal emperor **Akbar**, giving him his daughter in marriage. The alliance made the Kachwahas the most powerful Rajput house at the Mughal court. Bharmal's grandson, **Raja Man Singh I**, became one of Akbar's greatest generals. He commanded the Mughal army at **Haldighati** in 1576, governed Kabul, Bihar and Bengal, and held one of the highest ranks in the empire. It was Man Singh who, around **1592**, began the building of the palace on the ridge that we see today.

The story of the Sheesh Mahal, as the people of Amber tell it, begins with this great Raja. He had seen the palaces of emperors and the temples of every province from Kabul to Bengal. Now, the legend says, he wanted something no one had ever seen. He called his master builders to him and gave them a task.

"I want a chamber," the Raja said, "where the stars shine even in the daytime. When the queens sit there at night, I want them to see the sky around them, and when a single lamp is lit, I want the whole room to blaze like the heavens."

The chief architect bowed and promised to try. The tellers do not give his name. He was, they say, the most skilled craftsman in the kingdom, and craftsmen came from far and wide to work under him. He tried painted ceilings of blue and gold. He tried inlay of precious stones. He tried polished plaster that shone like marble. But every time the Raja came to look, the room was beautiful, and dark. Paint did not shine. Stones glittered only where the light fell directly. The months passed, and the architect grew afraid that he would fail his master.

In his despair, the legend says, he went to the shrine of **Lord Ganesha**, the remover of obstacles, the god whom every builder calls on before laying the first stone. He prayed late into the night, offering sweets and red flowers, and asked only to be shown the way. When at last he slept, he dreamed of a dark chamber, and in it a single small flame. As he watched, the flame was caught and thrown back, again and again, by thousands of tiny pieces of glass, set into the walls and ceiling like jewels, each one turned a little differently from the next, until the room was full of light like a sky full of stars.

He woke before dawn and called his craftsmen. They began to cut glass into small pieces of every shape: stars, flowers, leaves, diamonds and circles. Some were flat, some curved, some coloured. They set them by hand, piece by piece, into patterns in fine white plaster, so that each one caught the light at its own angle. It took a long time and endless patience, the story says, but when the last piece was set and a single lamp was lit in the dark, the room came alive. The light flashed back from the walls and the ceiling a thousand times over, and the chamber looked like the night sky on a clear winter evening. The Raja, the legend says, was so delighted that he ordered the architect to be weighed against gold, and gave him all of it.

That is the legend. The history is a little different, and in some ways even richer. The chamber of mirrors at Amber, the **Sheesh Mahal**, stands in the third courtyard of the palace, as part of the hall called the **Jai Mandir**. It was not built under Man Singh I but under one of his successors, his great-grandson **Mirza Raja Jai Singh I**, who ruled Amber from 1621 to 1667. Jai Singh I was a great commander in the service of the Mughal emperors **Shah Jahan** and **Aurangzeb**, and it was he who rebuilt and enlarged much of the palace, adding the courtyard of the Jai Mandir and its gardens and the splendid painted gateway called the **Ganesh Pol**, crowned with an image of Ganesha.

The art of mirror work, called *aina-kari*, was in high fashion at the Mughal court in those years. In the 1630s Shah Jahan built a famous Sheesh Mahal in the fort at Lahore, and nobles of the empire, Rajput and Mughal alike, decorated their own palaces in the same style. The Sheesh Mahal of Amber belongs to this world. Its walls and ceilings are covered with thousands of pieces of convex and coloured glass set into white plaster, shaped into flowers, vases and stars, together with panels of carved marble. And the effect that the legend describes is real. When the room is darkened and a single flame is lit, the light is reflected from the glass again and again, and the ceiling glitters like a starlit sky. Guides at Amber still demonstrate it to visitors.

So the legend has borrowed the name of the more famous Raja and set the story a generation or two too early. It sometimes also says that the emperor **Akbar** himself came to Amber to see the wonder. That cannot be so: Akbar died in 1605, long before the Sheesh Mahal was made. But the heart of the story, that the chamber's beauty came from patient craftsmen setting countless pieces of glass by hand, is true, and so is its connection to Ganesha, whose image watches over the gateway of the palace that Jai Singh I built.

Across the courtyard from the Jai Mandir stands the **Sukh Niwas**, the hall of pleasure, where water once ran in a marble channel through the room to cool the air in the burning summers. Between them lies a formal garden in the Mughal style. In the evenings of the seventeenth century, the courtyard would have been full of the sound of water and music, and the light of lamps would have shimmered in the mirrors of the Sheesh Mahal across the dark garden. It is easy to imagine how such a place gave birth to legends.

After Sawai Jai Singh II moved his capital to Jaipur in 1727, the palace of Amber grew quiet. But it was never abandoned. The Kachwaha rulers continued to come there for ceremonies, and the temple of **Shila Devi** within the palace, the family goddess of the house, remained a place of worship. In time, the Sheesh Mahal suffered from age and neglect; pieces of glass fell from the walls, and the plaster cracked. Careful restoration in modern times has brought much of it back, and since 2013 Amber has been one of the **Hill Forts of Rajasthan** listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Today visitors climb the ramp from Maota lake, pass beneath the Ganesh Pol, and step into the courtyard of the Jai Mandir. When they enter the Sheesh Mahal and look up at the glittering ceiling, many of them hear the story of the architect and his dream for the first time. Whether or not he ever lived, the legend says something true about the place: that its beauty came from the patience of human hands, and from the idea, so simple and so brilliant, that a single small flame, caught and thrown back a thousand times, could fill a whole room with stars.

## Remembered for

- **The architect's dream.** Legend says a master builder prayed to Ganesha and dreamed of covering the walls with countless pieces of glass so that one flame would shine like a thousand stars.
- **The reward in gold.** The tellers say the delighted Raja had the architect weighed against gold and gave him all of it.
- **The real builders.** Man Singh I began the palace around 1592; the Sheesh Mahal in the Jai Mandir was built under Mirza Raja Jai Singh I, who ruled from 1621 to 1667.
- **The art of aina-kari.** The chamber belongs to the Mughal-era fashion for mirror work, with thousands of pieces of convex and coloured glass set in white plaster.
- **A starlit ceiling.** The effect the legend describes is real: a single flame in the darkened room is reflected countless times, and guides still show it to visitors.
- **A correction to the tale.** Akbar could not have visited the Sheesh Mahal, as he died in 1605, before it was built.
- **World Heritage.** Amber is one of the Hill Forts of Rajasthan listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2013.

stories.title: The Secret Tunnel to Jaigarh
stories.story:
## The Secret Tunnel to Jaigarh — the hidden road beneath the Kachwaha hills

*The tunnel between Amber and Jaigarh is partly real and partly legend: a stretch of it can be walked today, while the stories of elephants, sealed chambers and endless passages belong to the folklore of Amer. Where history and legend part ways, this story says so.*

Long before there was a city called Jaipur, there was a narrow valley in the Aravalli hills where the road from Delhi to Ajmer squeezed between two ridges. Whoever held that valley held the road. The **Kachwaha** Rajputs, who traced their descent from Kush, the son of Rama, made it their home in the eleventh and twelfth centuries, when they took the old settlement of **Amber** from the Meena chiefs who had ruled it before them. For the next six hundred years Amber was the seat of their power.

The Amber that visitors see today is mostly younger than that. The great palace on the hillside, with its courtyards, gateways and mirrored halls, was begun by **Raja Man Singh I** around **1592**, when he was one of the greatest generals of the Mughal emperor Akbar, and it was enlarged by his successors, above all by **Mirza Raja Jai Singh I** in the seventeenth century. Above the palace, on the higher ridge called the Cheel ka Teela, the Hill of Eagles, stood the stronghold that would become **Jaigarh**. There had been fortifications on that summit for a long time, but the fort in its present form owes most to **Sawai Jai Singh II**, who completed it around **1726**.

The two forts were made to work as one. Amber was the palace, the place of court and family, of gardens and festivals. Jaigarh was the fist above it: a garrison, an armoury, a foundry for cannon and, tradition says, the treasury of the Kachwaha house. Look at the ridge from the lake below and you can see the long line of walls running up the hill from the palace to the summit, like a stone rope tying the two together. And somewhere inside that rope, the people of Amer have always said, runs a hidden road.

The old men of the town tell the story slowly, as if it were a secret they had been allowed to keep. In the days of Raja Man Singh, they say, the king called his master masons to the palace one evening. The empire was at peace, and the Kachwaha armies were far away in Kabul, in Bihar or in Bengal, fighting the emperor's wars. But a wise king, the story says, builds his escape before he needs it.

"If an enemy ever comes up this valley," the king is supposed to have said, "the palace will be the first thing he sees and the first thing he attacks. I want a road that no enemy can see. A road from my house to the summit, through the hill itself."

Whether any such conversation ever took place, no one can say. No document records an order to build a tunnel, and no inscription names the men who dug it. But a passage does exist. From the palace complex at Amber a fortified way climbs towards Jaigarh, partly cut into the hillside and partly roofed and enclosed by stone walls, so that men could move between the two forts without exposing themselves on the open slope. In recent years a section of this passage has been cleared and opened to visitors, who walk through its cool, dim length and come out high above the palace, closer to the walls of Jaigarh.

That much is history. Everything else belongs to the storytellers, and the storytellers of Amer have never been short of imagination.

In their version, the tunnel is not a modest passage but a road under the mountain more than two kilometres long, with chambers opening off it at intervals where guards could rest and stores could be kept. Shafts rise from these chambers to the surface, hidden among rocks and bushes, so that fresh air flows through the whole length. At secret points along the way, they say, there were doors to the outside, so cleverly made that from the hillside they looked like nothing more than boulders. And the passage, in the boldest telling, was so wide and so high that an elephant could walk through it with its howdah on its back.

No elephant has ever walked through the tunnel that can be seen today, and it is hard to imagine one doing so. The section open to visitors is built for people, not for the great beasts of the royal stables. But the story of the elephants tells us something about how the people of Amer thought of their kings. In their imagination nothing the Kachwahas built could be ordinary. If the kings had a secret road, it had to be fit for a royal procession.

The legends also give the tunnel a purpose, and that purpose is always the same: escape. Imagine, the storytellers say, a night of siege. The valley below is full of the campfires of an enemy army. The gates of the palace are shut, and the walls along the lake are lined with archers and matchlock men. In the zenana, the women's quarters, the queens and the children are woken in the dark. Lamps are shaded. Servants carry chests and bundles. A door that no one has noticed before is opened in a wall, and a line of figures disappears into the rock, climbing upwards in silence while the enemy waits below for a morning attack. By dawn the royal family is behind the far stronger walls of Jaigarh, with its cisterns full of water and its stores full of grain, and the palace below is only a house that can be rebuilt.

It is a powerful picture, and the logic behind it is sound. Jaigarh was the stronger fort. Its great water tanks could hold enough rain to supply a garrison for a long time, and its position on the summit made it very hard to approach. A covered route from the palace to the citadel was exactly the kind of thing a careful Rajput ruler would build. But the history of Amber does not record any night when the royal family fled through the tunnel from a besieging army. For most of the seventeenth century the Kachwahas were among the most powerful nobles of the Mughal Empire, and Amber was not besieged. The great crisis came in **1707–08**, after the death of Aurangzeb, when the new emperor **Bahadur Shah I** occupied Amber in his quarrel with Sawai Jai Singh II. Even then the story was one of politics and armies in the open, not of a secret flight underground, and Jai Singh recovered his capital within a year with the help of his Rathore allies.

The second purpose the legends give the tunnel is the movement of treasure. Jaigarh, tradition says, was where the Kachwahas kept their wealth, and the tunnel was the road along which it travelled. In the stories, men moved chests of gold coins and bags of jewels from the palace treasury up to the citadel by night, so that no spy in the valley would ever know how much the kings possessed or where it was kept. Here too the legend grows from something real. Rulers did keep treasuries in their strongest forts, and Jaigarh was the strongest fort the Kachwahas had. But no account survives of what was moved, when, or how.

The treasure stories became so famous that in the twentieth century they reached the government of India itself. In **1976**, during the Emergency, the government ordered a search of Jaigarh for the treasure that rumour said was hidden there. Teams dug and searched within the fort for months. The official conclusion was that no hidden treasure of the kind the legends described had been found. Far from ending the story, the search gave it new life, because people in Amer and Jaipur have argued about it ever since.

The tunnel stories have grown in the same way. Ask in the bazaars below the fort and you will hear that the part shown to tourists is only the beginning. The main passage, people say, branches off somewhere in the darkness and has never been found. Some say it leads to sealed rooms in which the oldest treasures and papers of the Kachwaha house still lie. Others say it does not stop at Jaigarh at all, but runs on through the hills to Nahargarh, or to caves deep in the Aravallis that only the old kings knew. A few insist that the old masons were sworn to silence, and that the secret died with them.

None of this can be confirmed, and the people who tell these stories usually do so with a smile. They know the difference between what they can show you and what they have heard from their grandfathers. But the stories persist because the landscape invites them. The hills around Amber are honeycombed with walls, gates, stepwells and watchtowers. The ridge-top walls run for kilometres, climbing and falling with the land. In such a place it is easy to believe that something more lies beneath the surface.

The real passage, though, has a story of its own that is worth telling. It shows how the Kachwahas thought about defence. They did not rely on a single great wall but on layers: the lake at the foot of the hill, the walled town, the palace with its gates, the fortified line along the ridges, and finally the citadel at the top. The covered passage linked the soft centre of this system, the palace, to its hard core, Jaigarh. In time of danger, men, messages and supplies could move between them without being seen from the valley. It was a practical work of military engineering, built by people who had served in the Mughal wars from Kabul to Bengal and knew what sieges looked like.

When Sawai Jai Singh II founded his new city of **Jaipur** on the plain below in **1727**, the court moved down from the hills. Amber became quieter, and the passage between the palace and Jaigarh lost its purpose. Jaigarh itself remained a garrison fort and arsenal of the Jaipur state, and Amber remained a place of temples and memory. For two centuries and more the tunnel was little more than a rumour in the town and a dark doorway that few people entered.

Today visitors walk through it with torches and phone lights, laughing at the echoes, pausing where the passage turns. Most of them do not know the old stories. But some, standing in the cool darkness with the rock pressing close on either side, find themselves listening for the sound of footsteps ahead of them: the soft steps of queens and servants climbing towards safety on a night that, as far as history knows, never came.

## Remembered for

- **A real covered passage.** A fortified route links the Amber palace with Jaigarh on the hill above, and part of it has been restored and opened to visitors.
- **Two forts as one system.** Amber was the palace and Jaigarh the citadel, arsenal and, by tradition, the treasury of the Kachwaha house.
- **The legend of the escape road.** Local stories describe a vast tunnel, wide enough for elephants, used by the royal family to flee a siege. No such flight is recorded in history.
- **Stories of moving treasure.** Tradition says the tunnel carried the Kachwaha wealth to Jaigarh by night; no record confirms it.
- **The 1976 search.** The government's search of Jaigarh for hidden treasure found nothing of the kind the legends describe, but kept the stories alive.
- **The endless passage.** Folk belief holds that the main tunnel remains undiscovered and runs on to sealed chambers or deep into the Aravallis.

stories.title: The Curse of the Sati
stories.story:
## The Curse of the Sati — the weeping queen of the zenana

*The story of the cursed queen of Amber is local folklore: no chronicle of the Kachwaha house names a queen called Ratnavati or records her condemnation, and the ghost stories are told by guards, guides and visitors, not by history. Where history and legend part ways, this story says so.*

The women's quarters of Amber lie at the very top and back of the palace, as far from the public courts as the builders could place them. To reach them a visitor passes through the great gateways, across the Diwan-i-Aam where the king once sat in public audience, through the gardens and mirrored halls of the private palace, and finally into a maze of small courtyards, narrow stairways and screened balconies. This is the oldest part of the palace that **Raja Man Singh I** began building around **1592**, and it was here that the queens, the princesses and their women lived their lives behind lattices of carved stone.

The zenana of Man Singh's palace was built around a single great courtyard, with a set of identical apartments opening onto it. Tradition says each was meant for one of the king's queens, and that the rooms were linked by corridors so that the king could visit any of them without the others knowing. Whatever the truth of that, the plan tells us something about the world of a Rajput palace at the height of the Mughal age. Man Singh was one of the most powerful men in the empire, a commander who fought for Akbar from Kabul to Bengal, and like other great nobles of his time he had many wives. Their lives were lived largely out of sight, and what happened inside those walls rarely entered the official record.

That silence is where the legend of the cursed queen was born.

The story, as the people of Amer tell it, begins in the years when the palace was still being built. Among the women of the zenana, they say, was a young queen of great beauty named **Ratnavati**. She had come to Amber as a bride from a distant house, and she was lonely in the great palace on the hill. She spent her days on the balconies looking out over Maota Lake and the valley beyond, singing softly to herself in the evenings, and the other women of the zenana did not like her.

Jealousy, in the old tales, is always the first poison. Whispers began to spread through the courtyards. Someone said Ratnavati had been seen speaking to a man at a window. Someone else said a message had been carried to her by a servant who would not say from whom. The whispers grew into accusations, and the accusations reached the ears of her husband.

Here the folk versions of the story differ, as folk stories do. In some tellings her husband falls ill and dies soon after, still believing she has betrayed him. In others he dies in war far away, and the news reaches Amber with the accusations still hanging over her head. All versions agree on what followed. When the funeral pyre was raised, the elders of the household decided that Ratnavati must ascend it. Her sati, they said, would wash away the stain of the accusation. If she was innocent, the fire would prove it. If she was guilty, the fire would cleanse her.

The storytellers describe the scene with great feeling. The queen is dressed in her bridal red. Her hands are marked with henna. The women who accused her stand at a distance, their faces hidden. Ratnavati walks to the pyre without weeping, but before she climbs it she turns and looks back at the palace on the hill.

"I go to the fire innocent," she says, in the words the tale gives her. "You have taken my life with lies. Let this house remember it. No woman within these walls will ever know lasting happiness while my name is unspoken."

Then she climbs the pyre, and the flames rise.

This is the curse as the legend tells it. It is important to say clearly what history can and cannot tell us about it. Sati, the burning of a widow on her husband's pyre, was a real and terrible practice in many Rajput royal houses of this period, and the Kachwaha house was no exception: the deaths of rulers were at times followed by the self-immolation of queens and concubines, and their memorials can be found in the cremation grounds of Rajasthan. But no chronicle of the Kachwahas names a queen called Ratnavati, and no record describes a queen of Amber forced onto the pyre because of an accusation of infidelity. The name Ratnavati itself appears in other folk tales of Rajasthan, most famously in the legend of the princess of Bhangarh. The story of Amber's cursed queen belongs to the world of folklore, where names and sorrows travel freely from one fort to another.

What the legend does reflect is real: the powerlessness of women in a world where reputation was everything, where a whisper could destroy a life, and where the fire was sometimes presented as a choice when it was really a sentence. Whether or not Ratnavati ever lived, many women of the Rajput courts faced pressures like hers, and the people of Amer, telling her story, may be remembering all of them.

After the curse, the legend says, Amber was never quite the same. And here the story moves from the past into the present, into the tales of the people who have worked and walked in the palace in more recent times.

The palace guards who kept watch at night in the old days, before Amber became a museum and a tourist site, are said to have been the first to see her. In the hour after midnight, they said, a woman in white would appear at the far end of a corridor in the zenana, walking slowly, her face covered by her veil. She would weep softly as she walked. If a guard called out to her, she would turn a corner and be gone, and when he reached the place there would be no one there and no door through which she could have passed.

Others have spoken of sounds rather than sights. In empty rooms of the zenana, people say, they have heard the soft clink of anklets and bangles, as if a woman were walking across the floor. They have heard the rustle of silk, the swish of a heavy skirt brushing against stone. On nights of the full moon, the stories go, there are sudden cold places in the corridors even in the heat of summer, and from somewhere above, from a balcony no one can reach, comes the sound of a woman's voice singing a slow, sad song in an old dialect, the same kind of song the young queen sang when she looked out over the lake.

Guides at Amber tell these stories to visitors, sometimes with a straight face and sometimes with a wink. Some women visitors say they feel uneasy in certain rooms of the old zenana, especially in the narrow passages where the light is dim and the walls are close. It is not hard to understand why. These are old rooms full of the memory of lives lived in confinement, and the imagination fills them easily. No investigation has ever confirmed any of these experiences, and there is no evidence that anything stranger than wind, echoes and human imagination is at work. But the stories keep being told.

It is also said that the priests of the temples of Amer have performed rites from time to time to bring peace to the restless spirit. In Rajasthan it is a common custom to honour those who died in sorrow or by violence, and many villages have shrines to such spirits. Whether a specific rite for Ratnavati has ever been performed at the palace is something only local people can say, and their accounts differ.

The boldest part of the legend claims that the curse was the real reason the Kachwahas left Amber. The rulers, it is said, could never find peace in a palace where a wronged queen walked at night, and so at last they moved their capital down to the plain. This, however, is folklore laid on top of a well-known historical event, and the history is quite different. When **Sawai Jai Singh II** founded **Jaipur** in **1727**, he did so for practical reasons. Amber was a hill town hemmed in by ridges, with little room to grow and a limited supply of water. The Kachwaha state had grown rich and populous, trade was increasing, and Jai Singh, a ruler deeply interested in astronomy, mathematics and planning, wanted a capital laid out on a grand and orderly plan on the open plain, with wide streets, markets and room for a growing population. Jaipur was the result, one of the best-planned cities of its time. No historical source connects the move to a curse.

Still, the legend endures, and in a way it has outlived the court it describes. The kings have gone to Jaipur and then into history. The zenana is empty, its rooms visited by tourists rather than queens. But on evenings when the crowds have left and the light turns gold over Maota Lake, when the shadows grow long in the narrow courtyards and the wind moves through the stone lattices with a sound almost like a sigh, it is easy to see why the people of Amer still speak of a woman in white who walks the corridors, waiting for someone to say that she was innocent.

## Remembered for

- **The zenana of Man Singh's palace.** The women's quarters at the back of the palace begun around 1592, built around a courtyard of separate apartments for the queens.
- **The legend of Ratnavati.** Folklore tells of a young queen falsely accused of infidelity and sent to the pyre. No Kachwaha record names her, and the name appears in other Rajasthani legends, including that of Bhangarh.
- **The curse.** Tradition says she declared that no woman in the palace would know lasting happiness.
- **The woman in white.** Guards and visitors tell of a weeping figure, the sound of anklets and silk, and a sad song on full-moon nights. None of this has ever been confirmed.
- **A memory of real suffering.** The tale reflects the real practice of sati in Rajput royal houses and the vulnerability of women in the courts.
- **The move to Jaipur.** Legend blames the curse, but Sawai Jai Singh II founded Jaipur in 1727 for space, water and growth.

stories.title: The Royal Elephant Procession
stories.story:
## The Royal Elephant Procession — the boy king who rode up the hill

*The accession of Jai Singh I is history; the golden procession of five hundred elephants is the memory of Amer's storytellers, and no contemporary account of it survives. Where history and legend part ways, this story says so.*

In the winter of **1621** the palace of Amber was in mourning. **Raja Bhao Singh**, the son of the great **Man Singh I**, had died after a short and unhappy reign, and he left no son to follow him. The Kachwaha throne passed instead to a boy of about eleven, **Jai Singh**, the grandson of Man Singh's eldest son Jagat Singh and the son of **Maha Singh**. In the language of the Mughal court, the Kachwaha ruler was not only a king in his own land but also a noble of the empire, and the succession had to be confirmed by the emperor **Jahangir**. The confirmation came, and the child who would one day be known across India as **Mirza Raja Jai Singh** became the lord of Amber.

The people of Amer remember his accession not by its date or its politics, but by a picture: a river of elephants climbing the hill.

The road to the palace has always been the same. From the shore of **Maota Lake**, a broad ramp of stone climbs in zigzags up the hillside, between walls and bastions, to the great eastern gateway, the **Suraj Pol**, the Gate of the Sun. Through that gate lies the **Jaleb Chowk**, the vast courtyard where soldiers paraded and where the king's processions gathered. Even today elephants carry visitors up this ramp in the morning, swaying slowly between the walls, and it takes no great imagination to see what the storytellers see when they speak of the day the boy king came home.

In their telling, the procession began at dawn. Below the hill, on the plain beside the lake, the elephants of the Kachwaha stables had been gathered, and with them the elephants of the nobles and the allied chiefs who had come to honour the new raja. The storytellers say there were five hundred of them. No document records the number, and it is likely that the storytellers have made it grow over the centuries, as storytellers do. But the Kachwaha house was rich and powerful, and its elephants were famous, and a great gathering for the accession of a ruler was the custom of the age.

Each elephant, the story goes, had been prepared for days. Their foreheads were painted in patterns of red, yellow and white. Their tusks were capped with bands of silver and brass. Over their backs lay heavy cloths of velvet and brocade, fringed with gold thread, that hung almost to the ground. Bells hung from their necks and anklets from their legs, so that as they moved the whole column sang with a deep, rolling music. The mahouts sat on their necks in turbans of saffron and red, and drummers and trumpeters rode on some of the beasts, playing as they climbed.

At the head of the column, in the legend, walked the greatest elephant of the royal stables, and on its back stood the royal howdah, which the storytellers describe as made of gold and set with jewels. In it sat the boy king, small and serious, dressed in the robes of his rank, with a turban jewel at his forehead. A guardian of the household sat beside him, for he was still a child and could not be left alone before such a crowd.

Whether the howdah was truly of solid gold, no one can say. Royal howdahs of the period were often covered with sheets of silver or gilded metal, and the most splendid had canopies of embroidered cloth and fittings of precious materials. The legend's solid gold is the kind of detail that grows naturally in the retelling of a great day.

The procession moved slowly. The ramp is steep and narrow at the turns, and elephants do not hurry. Behind the royal beast came the elephants of the nobles, each with its own banner and its own retinue. Then came horsemen, rows of foot soldiers with spears and matchlocks, standard-bearers, priests carrying offerings for the goddess, and musicians playing the *shehnai* and the *nagara*. Dancers moved in the spaces between the companies. And along the whole length of the road, the storytellers say, the people of Amber and the villages around it crowded every wall and every rooftop to see.

The legend says the procession was so long that six hours passed between the moment the first elephant reached the Suraj Pol and the moment the last one passed through it. Again, this is the measure of memory rather than of record. But anyone who has watched even a dozen elephants climb that ramp will understand why the people remembered the day as endless.

As evening came, the story goes, the walls of the palace and the ramparts along the ridges were lit with oil lamps, thousands of small flames in clay saucers set along every parapet. From the plain below, Amber seemed to float on the dark hill like a crown of fire, and the light could be seen from far across the valley. In the palace, the boy raja was seated before the household gods and the goddess **Shila Devi**, whose image Man Singh had brought to Amber, and received the homage of his nobles one by one.

The legend adds that European travellers saw the procession and wrote about it, and that its fame spread across the empire. This part of the story cannot be supported. A few European travellers did pass through Mughal India in these years, and some of them wrote about the court of Jahangir, but no known European account describes the accession of Jai Singh at Amber. The detail seems to have been added later, perhaps in the age when Amber had become famous among foreign visitors and it seemed natural to imagine that foreigners had always admired it.

What can be said with confidence is that the boy who rode up the hill that day grew into one of the most remarkable men of the seventeenth century. Jai Singh spent almost his whole life in the service of the Mughal emperors: first Jahangir, then **Shah Jahan**, and finally **Aurangzeb**. He fought on nearly every frontier of the empire, in the Deccan, in Central Asia during the Balkh campaign, and in the sieges of Kandahar. Shah Jahan gave him the title of **Mirza Raja**, and he rose to the highest ranks a noble could hold. He was famous as a diplomat as much as a soldier, and he spoke several languages.

His most famous campaign came near the end of his life. In **1665**, sent by Aurangzeb against **Shivaji**, he besieged the Maratha fort of Purandar and brought Shivaji to terms in the **Treaty of Purandar**, under which Shivaji surrendered many forts and agreed to visit the imperial court. The next year Shivaji went to Agra, where he was humiliated and placed under watch, in the custody of Jai Singh's son **Ram Singh**. His famous escape from Agra damaged Ram Singh's standing with the emperor, and Jai Singh himself, still fighting in the south, fell from favour. He died at **Burhanpur** in **1667**.

At Amber, Jai Singh's name is written into stone. Much of the palace that visitors see today grew in his time. The great hall of public audience, the **Diwan-i-Aam**, with its double rows of columns, is attributed to him, and so is the splendid **Ganesh Pol**, the painted gateway that leads into the private palace, with the image of Ganesha above its arch. Beyond it lies the **Jai Mandir**, whose walls and ceilings are covered with the tiny mirrors that give it the name **Sheesh Mahal**: in the light of a single candle, the guides say, the whole room glitters like the night sky. Whether every one of these buildings belongs to his reign exactly is debated, but together they reflect the wealth and taste of a Kachwaha court at the height of its Mughal service.

So the story of the elephant procession, even if its numbers are those of legend, is really a story about beginnings. It marks the moment when a child took the throne of a house that would, under his rule, reach the peak of its power within the empire. The people of Amer have kept the day alive not because anyone counted the elephants, but because the image fits what followed: a long, slow, magnificent climb.

And still, in the early mornings, when the elephants of Amer begin their slow walk up the ramp from the lake, with painted foreheads and swaying cloths and the sound of bells, some of the older guides will point to the gate above and tell their visitors that once, long ago, a boy of eleven rode up this road in a howdah of gold, and that the elephants behind him stretched all the way down to the water.

## Remembered for

- **The accession of Jai Singh I (1621).** After the death of Raja Bhao Singh without a son, the eleven-year-old grandson of Jagat Singh became ruler of Amber, confirmed by Jahangir.
- **The legend of the procession.** Tradition remembers a vast procession of decorated elephants climbing the ramp from Maota Lake to the Suraj Pol and the Jaleb Chowk.
- **The golden howdah and the lamps.** The storytellers tell of a jewelled howdah and ramparts lit with thousands of lamps. The numbers, the six hours and the European eyewitnesses are not supported by any surviving record.
- **Mirza Raja Jai Singh.** The boy king became one of the greatest Mughal commanders and diplomats, best known for the Treaty of Purandar with Shivaji in 1665.
- **Builder of Amber.** The Diwan-i-Aam, the Ganesh Pol and the mirrored Jai Mandir are associated with his reign.
- **The elephant road today.** Elephants still climb the same ramp each morning, keeping the old picture alive.

stories.title: The Hidden Treasure of Maota Lake
stories.story:
## The Hidden Treasure of Maota Lake — gold beneath the still water

*The sunken treasure of Maota Lake is a folk legend of Amer; no record describes chests sunk in the lake, and the old story's link to Aurangzeb does not fit the history. Where history and legend part ways, this story says so.*

At the foot of the hill of Amber lies a sheet of still water that holds the whole palace upside down. **Maota Lake** gathers the rain that runs off the surrounding hills, and in the monsoon it fills almost to the walls; in the dry months it shrinks back and leaves its edges bare and cracked. In the middle of it sits a garden laid out in geometric beds, the **Kesar Kyari**, the saffron garden, where tradition says the kings once tried to grow saffron. From the shore the reflection of Amber's yellow walls and the line of ramparts along the ridge shivers in the water whenever the wind moves. It is the most peaceful place in Amer. It is also, the people of the town will tell you, the place where the Kachwahas hid their gold.

The legend is told in the tea stalls along the lake road and repeated by boatmen and guides. It goes like this.

Once, in the days of the great kings, an emperor in Delhi grew angry with the house of Amber. He sent an army to take the fort and seize its treasury. Word came to Amber that the imperial forces were on the march, and the ruler gathered his most trusted men in a closed room of the palace at night.

"The fort may fall," he told them. "Forts have fallen before. But the wealth of this house will not fall with it. If they want our gold, let them look for it where no one will think to look."

Over the following nights, the story says, boats moved silently across the dark lake. Men carried chests up from the palace treasury, heavy with gold coins, jewellery, gem-set vessels and the precious objects of generations. The chests were loaded into the boats, rowed out to the deepest parts of the lake, and lowered one by one into the black water. No torches were lit. Only a handful of officials knew where each chest went down, and they swore an oath never to speak of it.

When the enemy army arrived, the legend continues, it found the treasury empty. The soldiers searched the palace and the fort, tore up floors and broke into walls, and found nothing. And so the treasure stayed in the lake, waiting for the day when it could safely be raised.

That day never came. The officials who knew the secret died, one by one. The story says the location of the chests was recorded in a code hidden in the decorations of the **Sheesh Mahal**, the hall of mirrors in the palace above, among its flowers, vines and tiny glittering panes, so that only a person who knew the key could read it. But the key was lost, and the mirrors keep their secret.

This is the legend. Now consider the history behind it.

The old version of the story names the emperor as **Aurangzeb**, and that is the first thing that does not fit. During Aurangzeb's long reign, from 1658 to 1707, the Kachwahas of Amber were not his enemies but among the most important nobles of his empire. **Mirza Raja Jai Singh I** led his armies in the Deccan and negotiated the Treaty of Purandar with Shivaji in 1665. His son **Ram Singh I** also served the emperor, even if he lost favour after Shivaji's escape from Agra. Relations were sometimes cold, and Aurangzeb's reign was a hard time for many Rajput houses, but there was no imperial army sent to take Amber and seize its treasury.

There was, however, a moment when Amber truly was taken by a Mughal emperor, and it may be the real event behind the legend. After Aurangzeb died in **1707**, his sons fought for the throne. The young ruler of Amber, **Sawai Jai Singh II**, supported the prince **Azam Shah**, who was defeated and killed by his brother at the battle of Jajau. The victor, **Bahadur Shah I**, punished Jai Singh. In **1707–08** he marched to Amber, took the town, gave the throne to Jai Singh's younger brother, and placed the capital under an imperial officer. Tradition says Amber was even given a new name, **Mominabad**, for a time.

Jai Singh did not accept this. He joined forces with **Ajit Singh** of Marwar, who had his own quarrel with the emperor, and with the support of other Rajput houses the allies drove out the imperial officers. Within a year, in **1708**, Jai Singh was back in Amber.

It is easy to see how a story of hidden treasure could grow from this real crisis. A ruler facing the loss of his capital would certainly have tried to protect his wealth, and moving valuables out of the reach of an occupying force would have been a sensible thing to do. But no record describes what Jai Singh did with the Kachwaha treasury in those months, and there is nothing to suggest that anything was sunk in Maota Lake. The legend, as so often in Rajasthan, has taken a real moment of danger and given it a secret ending.

The second part of the legend, the code in the Sheesh Mahal, belongs entirely to the imagination. The mirrored hall, with its convex glass set in plaster, its painted flowers and its tiny inlaid patterns, is so intricate that it invites the idea of hidden meanings. Visitors stand in it looking up at the ceiling, and it is only natural to wonder whether the patterns are trying to say something. But its decoration follows the conventions of Rajput and Mughal palace art of its time, and no one has ever shown that it contains a map of anything.

Over the centuries, the legend says, many people have come to the lake hoping to find what the kings left behind. Men are said to have dived into its murky water in the dry season, prodding the mud with sticks, and to have dug along its edges at night. Some, the story goes, came back with a handful of old coins or a broken ornament, and each small find was enough to convince the town that the great chests were still down there, just out of reach. Whether any of these finds were real, or where they truly came from, no one can say. Old coins turn up in many places in a town that has been lived in for a thousand years.

The lake and the fort are today protected parts of a heritage site that belongs to the public, and no one is free to go digging in them for treasure. That, too, has become part of the legend. If the authorities guard the lake, people say with a knowing look, perhaps they have a reason.

There is another kind of treasure in the story, and it is real. Maota Lake was never just a pretty mirror for the palace. It was part of how Amber survived. In a dry land, water was life, and the lake, together with the tanks and channels around the fort, stored the rain that the town and the palace needed through the long months without it. Water was raised from the lake to the palace gardens, and the Kesar Kyari and the **Dilaram Bagh** beside it were watered from it. When the old kings looked down from their balconies at the lake, they were looking at the source of their palace's life as much as at a beautiful view.

So when the boatmen of Amer tell their visitors about the gold beneath the water, they are, without knowing it, telling a deeper truth. The wealth of Amber did depend on Maota Lake. It just did not lie at the bottom of it.

On quiet evenings, when the last visitors have left and the reflection of the palace lights trembles on the dark surface, the people of the town still look out over the water and wonder. Somewhere out there, the story says, the chests are waiting in the mud, their gold dull and green with age, their locks rusted shut, guarding the secret of a king who chose to give his treasure to the lake rather than to his enemies.

## Remembered for

- **Maota Lake.** The rain-fed lake at the foot of Amber, with the Kesar Kyari garden in its centre, which gave the palace water and its famous reflection.
- **The legend of the sunken chests.** Folklore says the Kachwahas sank their treasure in the lake by night to save it from an invading emperor.
- **A corrected history.** Aurangzeb never sent an army to take Amber. The real crisis came in 1707–08, when Bahadur Shah I occupied Amber and Sawai Jai Singh II recovered it with Rathore help in 1708.
- **The code of the Sheesh Mahal.** Tradition claims the treasure map was hidden in the mirrored hall's decoration; nothing supports this.
- **Treasure hunters and small finds.** Stories of coins and ornaments found in the mud keep the legend alive, though none has been linked to a royal hoard.
- **The real treasure.** The lake's true value was its water, which sustained the palace and its gardens.

stories.title: The Diplomatic Marriage Alliance
stories.story:
## The Diplomatic Marriage Alliance — how a wedding at Sambhar changed Amber

*The alliance of 1562 between Raja Bharmal and Akbar is well recorded in Mughal histories such as Abul Fazl's Akbarnama; the name of the bride and the inner life of the court are less certain. Where history and legend part ways, this story says so.*

In the middle of the sixteenth century, Amber was a small kingdom in serious trouble. The Kachwaha Rajputs had ruled the hill country around it for centuries, but they were not yet one of the great houses of Rajasthan. Their neighbours in Mewar and Marwar were older, richer and more famous. Worse, the house of Amber was divided against itself.

The trouble began with a disputed succession. After the death of **Raja Prithviraj** in the 1520s, the throne passed among his sons amid quarrels and rivalries. By the late 1540s it had come to **Raja Bharmal**, one of the younger sons. But Bharmal's nephew **Sujamal**, the son of his elder brother Puranmal, believed the throne was rightfully his. Sujamal found a powerful backer: **Mirza Sharafuddin Husain**, the Mughal governor of the region around Ajmer and Mewat, a restless and ambitious noble who saw in the Kachwaha quarrel a chance to extend his own power.

Sharafuddin pressed Amber hard. His troops raided Kachwaha lands, and he took members of Bharmal's family as hostages to force the raja's submission. Bharmal was caught between an ambitious Mughal officer on one side and a rival kinsman on the other, with no great Rajput power willing to save him. He needed a protector stronger than Sharafuddin, and there was only one: the young emperor himself.

In January **1562**, **Akbar**, then about nineteen years old, set out from Agra on a pilgrimage to the shrine of the Sufi saint **Khwaja Muinuddin Chishti** at Ajmer. His road passed close to Kachwaha country. The Mughal histories tell how a noble of the court, Chaghatai Khan, brought word of Bharmal's plight to the emperor, and how Bharmal came to meet Akbar on the road with his kinsmen. The raja offered his loyalty, and to bind that loyalty in the most solemn way known to the age, he offered his eldest daughter in marriage.

Akbar accepted. On his return journey from Ajmer, the marriage took place at **Sambhar**, beside the great salt lake, in **February 1562**. Bharmal's son **Bhagwant Das** and his young grandson **Man Singh** entered the emperor's service and travelled with him back to Agra. Sharafuddin's pressure on Amber ended, and soon afterwards the Mughal noble himself rebelled against Akbar and fled.

We can imagine the scene at Sambhar: the flat white shore of the lake shimmering in the winter sun, the tents of the imperial camp, the Rajput horsemen in their saffron turbans arriving with the bride's party, the drums of both camps, the elders of Amber grave and uncertain. Bharmal is said to have known that he was taking a step his neighbours would condemn. Some of the proudest Rajput houses, above all Mewar, would refuse marriage alliances with the Mughals for generations and look down on those who made them. But Bharmal also knew that his house might not survive without a powerful friend.

One can picture, too, the moment of parting, as every Rajput wedding song remembers it. The bride's mother holds her daughter for the last time. The women of the household sing the old songs of farewell, in which a daughter is a bird who flies from her father's courtyard to a stranger's house. A curtained litter waits at the edge of the camp. This time the stranger's house was the court of an emperor, far away in Agra, and the daughter of Amber was going into a world whose language, food and faith were all different from her own. Whatever the politics, it was a young woman who carried the weight of the alliance.

The bride is remembered in Mughal history by the title **Mariam-uz-Zamani**, "Mary of the Age", which she received later. Her personal name is uncertain. Later tradition has given her names such as **Harka Bai** and **Hira Kunwari**, but these do not appear in the histories of Akbar's own time, and the question is still debated. In **1569**, at Sikri, she gave birth to Akbar's son **Salim**, the prince who would rule as the emperor **Jahangir**. She remained an important and wealthy figure at court for decades, engaged in trade and patronage, and outlived her husband by many years.

The story told at Amber often describes this as the first marriage between a Rajput princess and a Muslim ruler, but that is not correct. Marriages between Rajput families and Muslim ruling houses had taken place long before, under the Delhi Sultanate and in the regional sultanates of Gujarat and Malwa. What was new was the scale and the meaning of what followed. Akbar did not treat the Kachwahas as a defeated people who had handed over a daughter. He treated them as kinsmen and gave them high rank, command of armies and a place at the centre of the empire. Their women were allowed to keep their own religion within the imperial household. The alliance became the model for a new relationship between the Mughals and the Rajput houses.

For the Kachwahas, the rewards were enormous. Bhagwant Das became one of Akbar's leading nobles. In 1585 his daughter, **Man Bai**, was married to Prince Salim, and she became the mother of Salim's eldest son, Khusrau. But the greatest beneficiary was Man Singh.

Man Singh grew up at the Mughal court and became one of the most trusted and able generals of the empire. In **1576** he commanded the imperial army against **Maharana Pratap** of Mewar at **Haldighati**, a battle that set the two great Rajput houses on opposite sides and that is still remembered with deep feeling in Rajasthan. He later served on the north-western frontier and as governor of **Kabul**, then of **Bihar**, and then of **Bengal**, where he fought long campaigns against the Afghan chiefs of the east. He rose to the rank of seven thousand, among the highest held by any noble of the empire. When Bhagwant Das died in **1589**, Man Singh succeeded him as raja of Amber.

His wealth and his travels transformed his home. Around **1592** Man Singh began building a new palace on the hillside of Amber, high above Maota Lake, the core of the great complex that stands today. Its builders drew on the traditions of Rajput palaces, with their courtyards, screened balconies and fortified gateways, and on the Mughal architecture Man Singh had seen at Agra, Fatehpur Sikri and Lahore, with its arched halls, pillared pavilions and formal gardens. The blend of the two became the style of Amber, later enriched by his successors.

Man Singh was also a devout patron of Hindu religion. He built the great temple of **Govind Dev** at Vrindavan, and tradition says that he brought the image of the goddess **Shila Devi** from Bengal and installed it in a temple within the palace at Amber, where she is still worshipped. Near the palace stands the graceful **Jagat Shiromani** temple, which tradition says was built by his queen in memory of their son Jagat Singh, who died young. The Mughal alliance, in other words, did not make the Kachwahas less Rajput or less Hindu. It made them rich enough to build on a grand scale.

The current story at Amber says that the alliance brought a long peace to the region, and in one sense it did: the Kachwaha lands, now protected by the empire, were spared the constant warfare of earlier decades, and trade along the road from Agra to Ajmer flourished. But it is important to remember the other side. Many Rajput houses gradually followed the Kachwaha example, entering Mughal service, while Mewar resisted for decades, and wars such as Haldighati showed how bitterly the alliance divided Rajput from Rajput. For some it was a wise act of statecraft that saved a kingdom. For others it was a surrender of pride. That argument has never quite ended.

What is beyond argument is what the marriage at Sambhar meant for Amber itself. A small, threatened hill kingdom became, within a generation, one of the most powerful houses in India. Its rajas commanded armies from Kabul to Bengal and stood close to the throne of the emperor. The palace they built on the hillside, with its golden walls reflected in the lake below, is the most visible result. Every courtyard and gateway of Amber, in a sense, begins with a worried raja meeting a young emperor on the road to Ajmer, and with a wedding on the shore of a salt lake in the winter of 1562.

## Remembered for

- **A kingdom in crisis.** Raja Bharmal faced a rival claim from his nephew Sujamal and pressure from the Mughal governor Mirza Sharafuddin Husain.
- **The meeting on the road to Ajmer (1562).** Bharmal met Akbar during the emperor's pilgrimage and offered his loyalty and his daughter's hand.
- **The marriage at Sambhar.** The wedding took place in February 1562. The bride, later titled Mariam-uz-Zamani, became the mother of Jahangir; her personal name is uncertain.
- **Not the first, but the most important.** Rajput–Muslim marriages had happened before, but this alliance shaped Mughal–Rajput relations for over a century.
- **The rise of Man Singh.** Bharmal's grandson became one of the empire's greatest generals and governors, and raja of Amber from 1589.
- **The palace of Amber.** Begun by Man Singh around 1592, it blends Rajput and Mughal architecture, funded by the wealth of imperial service.
