stories.title: The Creation of Jaivana Cannon
stories.story:
## The Creation of Jaivana Cannon — the giant of the Hill of Eagles

*Jaivana is real and still stands on the ramparts of Jaigarh; the master founder Gopal Singh, his son's sacrifice and the crater from its single shot belong to local legend, and no record confirms them. Where history and legend part ways, this story says so.*

High on the ridge above Amber, on the hill the people of the region call the **Cheel ka Teela**, the Hill of Eagles, stands **Jaigarh**, the fort that guarded the Kachwaha capital. Its walls run along the crest for kilometres, and from its towers a watchman can see the palace of Amber far below, the long valley of the Delhi road, and on clear days the plain where the city of Jaipur now spreads. In one corner of the fort, under a raised shelter on the eastern ramparts, rests the thing that most visitors climb the hill to see: an enormous cannon on a wheeled carriage, its barrel pointing out over the hills. Its name is **Jaivana**, "the arrow of victory".

Jaivana was cast in **1720**, in the reign of **Sawai Jai Singh II**, the most brilliant ruler of the Kachwaha house. Jai Singh was a soldier and statesman, but he was also a scholar of astronomy and mathematics who built great stone observatories, the **Jantar Mantar**, at Jaipur, Delhi, Ujjain, Varanasi and Mathura, and who planned the city of Jaipur on a new and orderly design. He was interested in everything that could be measured and made, and the weapons of war were no exception. Under him Jaigarh became not only a fortress but also an arsenal and a foundry, where guns were cast for the armies of Amber.

The foundry can still be seen inside the fort. Here metal was melted in a furnace, poured into moulds sunk into pits in the ground, and allowed to cool before the barrel was raised, bored and finished. There is a long-standing local tradition that the barrels were bored with machinery turned by bullocks, and the fort still displays a great wheel said to have been used for this. Jaivana was the largest thing ever made there, and the effort it took explains why so much legend has gathered around it.

The figures usually given for the cannon are impressive. Its barrel is about six metres long, and the whole gun is commonly said to weigh around fifty tonnes. It is often described as the largest cannon on wheels of its age. It was meant, tradition says, to fire balls of fifty kilograms or more. These numbers are repeated on signboards and in guidebooks, and they give a sense of the scale of the work, even if the exact measurements vary from one account to another.

Around this real achievement, the people of Amer and Jaipur have woven a story that is far darker than anything in the records.

In their telling, Maharaja Jai Singh decided that his kingdom needed a weapon so great that no enemy would ever dare to approach his capital. He summoned the finest metalworkers and gun-founders from his own lands and from far beyond, and he set over them a master craftsman whom the story calls **Gopal Singh**. Gopal Singh was old and famous. His guns stood on the walls of many forts, and he was said to understand metal the way a priest understands scripture.

Gopal Singh listened to the king's command in silence. Then, the story says, he bowed his head and spoke.

"Maharaj, I can make you such a gun. But metal of this size is not like other metal. It has a will of its own. The old masters of my craft say that a weapon this great will not hold together unless it is given a life. Without a sacrifice, it will crack in the mould or burst at the first firing."

The king, in the legend, was troubled. He did not want blood spilled for his cannon. But before he could answer, Gopal Singh's own son, a young man who worked beside his father in the foundry, stepped forward.

"Let it be me," he said. "If my life makes the gun strong, then my life will guard this kingdom for as long as the gun stands."

The storytellers say the father wept but did not stop him. The son's sacrifice, in the tale, took place at the casting pit before the molten metal was poured. Then the furnace was opened, and the bright river of metal ran down into the mould while the whole foundry stood silent.

It must be said plainly: there is no historical evidence for any of this. No document of Jai Singh's reign names a founder called Gopal Singh, and there is no record of any human sacrifice at the casting of Jaivana. Stories of sacrifice at the founding of great works, whether forts, bridges, tanks or bells, are found in many parts of India and the world. They are a way of saying that something was so difficult, so dangerous and so costly that it seemed to demand a life. The legend of Jaivana belongs to that old family of tales.

The legend says the work took seven years, with men toiling day and night. The real casting may have taken far less time, though the preparation of the mould, the gathering of metal and the finishing of a barrel of this size would certainly have been long and difficult work. The tale also speaks of a special alloy whose secret recipe died with the master. Again, no record survives of the exact process, and the stories have filled the silence.

The most famous part of the legend is the firing. Jaivana, it is said, was fired only once, as a test. The tale tells that the men who loaded it were careful to stand well away, and that the soldiers who fired it jumped into water tanks to protect themselves from the shock. The ball, the story goes, flew some thirty-five kilometres and came down near the town of **Chaksu**, south of Jaipur, where it struck the earth so hard that it made a hollow that filled with water and became a pond. The roar of the gun, people say, was heard a hundred kilometres away, and in the villages near the fort the shock cracked walls and frightened animals.

These claims are told with great enthusiasm, but they cannot be confirmed. A smoothbore cannon of the early eighteenth century, however large, could not have reached anything like that distance, and no contemporary record describes the test firing or its results. The pond at Chaksu is a fine story, and people in the area still point it out, but it is not evidence. What can be said is that the cannon was never fired in war.

That last fact is one of the reasons Jaivana became so famous. It was never needed. In the years after it was cast, Jaipur faced pressures from many directions, including the rise of Maratha power in the eighteenth century, but no army ever came against Jaigarh in a way that would have tested its great gun. The legend turns this into a moral: the cannon was so terrible that its mere presence kept enemies away. It is a pleasing idea, and perhaps there is some truth in the thought that a fort known to hold such a weapon was not an easy target. But the real reasons Jaigarh was never besieged had more to do with the politics of the time and the strength of the Kachwaha state than with one gun.

As for Gopal Singh, the legend ends quietly. The king, it says, rewarded him with land and gold, and honoured him before the whole court. But the old founder never cast another weapon. He spent his remaining years in mourning, sitting in the evenings on the ramparts beside the great gun, looking out at the hills where his son's life, as he believed, now kept watch. When he died, the story goes, his ashes were scattered from those walls.

Today Jaivana rests under its shelter, cleaned and painted, with its great wheels and its long dark barrel. Visitors stand beside it and are photographed, small against its bulk. The guides tell the official facts first: cast in 1720, in the reign of Sawai Jai Singh II, in the foundry of this fort, never used in war. Then, if the visitors seem interested, they lower their voices a little and tell the other story, of the old master and the son who stepped forward, of the single shot and the pond far away.

The visitors cannot know which version to believe, and perhaps that does not matter. The real Jaivana is remarkable enough: a giant of metal made by the craftsmen of an eighteenth-century Rajput kingdom, a sign of Jai Singh's ambition and of the skill of the men who served him. The legend adds what the records leave out, the feeling that something so great must have cost something just as great, and that behind every wonder of stone and metal stand people whose names history has forgotten.

## Remembered for

- **A real giant.** Jaivana was cast in 1720 at Jaigarh's own foundry under Sawai Jai Singh II and is often described as the largest cannon on wheels of its age.
- **The foundry of Jaigarh.** The fort was an arsenal where cannon were cast and bored, and its casting pits and great wheel can still be seen.
- **The legend of Gopal Singh.** Folklore tells of a master founder whose son gave his life so the cannon would be strong. No record names Gopal Singh or confirms any sacrifice.
- **The single shot.** Tradition says the cannon was test-fired once and its ball fell near Chaksu, forming a pond. This is not supported by any record and is far beyond the range of such a gun.
- **Never fired in war.** Jaivana was never used in battle. Legend says its presence alone was enough to keep enemies away.
- **A father's mourning.** The tale ends with the old founder grieving beside the gun, a memory of the human cost behind great works.

stories.title: The Hidden Treasury Chambers
stories.story:
## The Hidden Treasury Chambers — the secret beneath the Hill of Eagles

*That Jaigarh was the strongroom of the Kachwahas is an old and widely held tradition, and the government's search of the fort in 1976 is a matter of record; the vaults, the sealed passages and the lost code belong to legend. Where history and legend part ways, this story says so.*

For most of its history, Jaigarh was a closed fort. Its gates opened for soldiers, for the officers of the garrison, for the men who worked the foundry and the stores, and for very few others. The people of Amer looked up at its long walls on the ridge above the palace and knew that it held the guns that guarded their town. But they also believed, and their grandparents had believed before them, that it held something more: the treasure of the Kachwaha kings.

The tradition is very old. The Kachwahas of Amber grew rich in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries through their service to the Mughal emperors. **Raja Man Singh I** commanded imperial armies from Kabul to Bengal; **Mirza Raja Jai Singh I** fought in the Deccan, in Central Asia and at Kandahar. The wealth that came to Amber from these campaigns, from rank, from land grants and, the stories say, from the spoils of war, had to be kept somewhere safe. The palace of Amber, beautiful as it was, lay on the lower slope of the hill. Jaigarh, on the summit above it, was the natural strongroom.

There is a well-known tradition about how that treasure was guarded. It is said that the treasury in the fort was placed in the care of trusted **Meena** chiefs, whose ancestors had ruled Amber before the Kachwahas and who remained bound to the royal house by ancient ties of service. According to this tradition, each new ruler of Amber was allowed to enter the treasury only once in his life, and to take a single object from it for himself. The rest remained under guard, untouched, for the safety of the kingdom. No document of the court has been published that confirms this custom, and historians treat it as tradition, but it is told so widely that it has become part of the identity of the fort.

From this tradition grew the legend of the hidden chambers.

In the tale as it is told today, **Sawai Jai Singh II**, who gave Jaigarh much of its present shape in the early eighteenth century, was a man who planned for every danger. He had seen his own capital taken from him by the emperor Bahadur Shah in 1707, and he had won it back only with the help of his allies. He did not intend to be caught unprepared again. So, the legend says, he ordered a secret treasury built deep beneath the fort.

The storytellers describe it with loving detail. The main vault, they say, lay thirty metres below the foundations, cut into the living rock of the hill. It could be reached only through a chain of hidden doors and passages, some disguised as blank walls, some opened by mechanisms of counterweights and stone pivots that only the builders understood. Each door led to another passage, each passage to another door, and a stranger who found the first entrance would lose himself long before he reached the last. Only one man knew the whole route: the chief treasurer, a retainer whose family had served the Kachwahas for generations, and who, in the tale, was sworn to pass the secret only to his own successor.

There is nothing in the historical record to support this description. No plan of such vaults is known, no account of their construction survives, and the scale the legend gives them is far beyond anything that has been found at Jaigarh. But the fort does contain something real that helps explain why the stories took hold. Beneath its courtyards lie enormous **underground water tanks**, great covered cisterns fed by channels that brought rainwater down from the surrounding slopes. They were built to keep the garrison supplied through long sieges, and their size is astonishing: dark, echoing chambers with vaulted roofs and pillars, big enough to hold the rain of a whole monsoon. To people who had never seen inside them, and who heard only that there were vast hidden rooms beneath the fort, it would have been easy to believe that something other than water was stored there.

The legend continues into more recent times. When the British became the dominant power in India, it says, the royal family feared that the treasure would be seized. So they moved what remained of it into the deepest chambers and sealed the passages forever. The location, the story claims, was hidden in a series of frescoes and carvings throughout the fort, a code that only the treasurer could read. When the last treasurer died without passing on the key, the secret died with him.

Here too history tells a different story. Jaipur was never taken over by the British. In **1818** the state signed a treaty with the East India Company, as many Rajput states did in those years, accepting British protection and paramountcy while keeping its own rulers and its own administration. The Maharajas of Jaipur continued to rule their state under this arrangement until **1949**, when Jaipur joined the new state of Rajasthan within independent India. There was no British seizure of the royal treasury and no moment of panic in which it had to be hidden from them. The tale of the sealed vaults has borrowed the fear of foreign power without the event that would have caused it.

Yet the legend did lead to one real and extraordinary episode. In **1976**, during the Emergency, the government of India launched a search for the treasure that rumour said lay hidden at Jaigarh. Teams worked inside the fort for months, digging, measuring and exploring, and the area around the fort was closely guarded while the search went on. The rumours of the time were wild. Some said the army had found gold and carried it away by night along the Jaipur–Delhi road. Others said they had found nothing at all. The government's official position was that no treasure of the kind described had been found at the fort.

The search did not settle the question in the minds of the people. If anything, it made the legend stronger. Why, people asked, would the government search for months if there were nothing to find? And if something had been found, would anyone ever say so? To this day, if you ask in the bazaars of Amer and Jaipur, you will hear every possible answer, told with equal confidence.

The legend also describes what the treasure contains. In the stories, it includes great quantities of gold, the famous jewels of the Kachwaha house, and ancient manuscripts of the royal library. Some tellers speak of diamonds of fabulous size. None of this has ever been seen or documented. The real wealth of the Jaipur royal family, its jewels, manuscripts, paintings and arms, is known in part from the collections of the City Palace and other records, and none of it needs a hidden vault to explain it.

Over the years, the legend says, treasure hunters have come to Jaigarh in secret, hoping to find what the government missed. Some are said to have found a few coins or small pieces of jewellery hidden in the walls, and each such find has been enough to keep the story alive. Whether these finds were real, and where they really came from, is impossible to say.

Today Jaigarh is open to visitors. They walk its ramparts, admire the great cannon Jaivana, look down into the dark water tanks, and wander through the old armoury and the rooms of the garrison. Guides point to the tanks and tell the story of the 1976 search. Some visitors look at the walls as they pass, as if a loose stone might open onto a hidden staircase, and some stand at the edge of a cistern and peer into the darkness, half hoping to see a glint of gold beneath the water.

What lies beneath Jaigarh, in truth, is rock, water and the foundations of a fort that did its work well, guarding a capital that it was never called on to defend in a great siege. But the legend of the hidden treasury chambers will not go away, because it answers a question that people have always asked about this fort: why it was so jealously guarded, and why so few were ever allowed inside. The answer the storytellers give is gold. The answer history gives is power, and the careful habits of a royal house that had learned, over many centuries, never to leave its most precious things where its enemies could reach them.

## Remembered for

- **The strongroom of the Kachwahas.** Tradition holds that Jaigarh, high above Amber, kept the treasure of the royal house.
- **The guardianship of the Meenas.** A widely told tradition says Meena chiefs guarded the treasury and each ruler could enter it once to take a single object; no court record confirms the custom.
- **The legend of the deep vaults.** Folklore describes secret chambers far below the fort, reached by hidden doors known only to the chief treasurer. Nothing of the kind has been found.
- **The real hidden rooms.** Jaigarh's huge underground water tanks, built for siege, help explain why such legends took hold.
- **A corrected history.** Jaipur was never annexed by the British; it accepted British protection by treaty in 1818 and joined Rajasthan in 1949.
- **The 1976 search.** The government's months-long search found no treasure of the kind the legend describes, but the story lives on.

stories.title: The Phantom Guard of Jaigarh
stories.story:
## The Phantom Guard of Jaigarh — the sentinel who never left his post

*The tale of Ram Singh, the guard who died at the gate of Jaigarh, is a folk legend of Amer; no record names him or describes a siege in which Jaigarh's gate was stormed, and the sightings of his ghost are stories, not evidence. Where history and legend part ways, this story says so.*

Night comes early to the Hill of Eagles. When the sun drops behind the western ridges, the long walls of **Jaigarh** turn from gold to grey, and then to black against the sky. The wind rises along the crest, moving through the gaps in the battlements and the empty rooms of the old garrison with a low, hollow sound. Far below, the lights of Amer come on one by one around the dark mirror of Maota Lake, and farther still the glow of Jaipur spreads across the plain. On the ramparts there is no light at all, except the stars.

It is on nights like these, the people of Amer say, that the guard walks.

Jaigarh was built to be watched over. It stands on the summit above the palace of Amber, the strongest point in the defences of the Kachwaha capital. There had been fortifications on this hill for a long time, but the fort as it stands today owes most to **Sawai Jai Singh II**, who completed much of it around **1726**. It held the arsenal and the cannon foundry of the state, the great underground water tanks that could supply a garrison through a long siege, and, tradition says, the treasury of the royal house. Its gates were guarded day and night. Soldiers lived within its walls for generations, and they kept their own stories, passed from the old men of the garrison to the young recruits on cold nights of watch. One of those stories is the tale of **Ram Singh**.

The legend places him in the eighteenth century, a time of real turmoil in the Jaipur state. After the death of Sawai Jai Singh II in 1743, his sons **Ishwari Singh** and **Madho Singh** fought for the throne, and both called in outside allies, including Maratha armies, who returned again and again in the following decades to demand tribute. Armies crossed the Kachwaha lands, and the safety of the capital could not be taken for granted. It was a time when every garrison had to be ready.

Into this troubled time the storytellers set their tale. Ram Singh, they say, was a Rajput of a poor family from a village in the hills, who had come to Jaigarh as a young man and served there all his life. He was not a noble or a famous captain. He was a gatekeeper, a man whose whole world was the great wooden gate studded with iron spikes, the heavy bar that held it shut, and the narrow stretch of wall above it. He was known for two things: he never slept on watch, and he never left his post without being relieved.

One night, the legend says, an enemy army came up the hills in the dark. The tale does not name them clearly. In some versions they are raiders, in others the soldiers of a rival claimant, in others a foreign force. They had learned that much of the garrison was away, and they meant to take the fort by surprise. By the time the alarm sounded, the enemy was already at the foot of the walls.

The captain of the fort, the story goes, looked out at the torches massing below and judged that the fort could not be held. He sent word along the walls that the gates should be opened and terms sought, so that the lives of the garrison would be spared. The message reached the main gate, where Ram Singh stood with only a handful of men.

The storytellers give him words that are still repeated in Amer.

"This gate was given to me to guard," he said. "It was not given to me to open. If the captain wants it opened, let him come and open it over my body."

And he did not move.

In the tale, the enemy reached the gate and found it shut. They tried to break it, and Ram Singh and his few companions held them back from the wall above with arrows, stones and matchlocks. When the attackers brought ladders, he cut them down. His companions fell one by one, but Ram Singh fought on alone through the night. Meanwhile, the legend says, the royal family who were in the fort that night were led away through hidden passages to safety, and every hour he held the gate was an hour more for their escape.

When dawn came, reinforcements arrived from the valley below and the enemy withdrew. The soldiers who climbed to the gate found Ram Singh dead at his post, standing against the wall, his sword still raised in his hand. The gate had held.

They buried him, the legend says, with full honours within the walls of the fort, close to the gate he had kept.

It is important to be clear about what history can say of this. Jaigarh was never captured in war, and there is no record of a night assault in which its main gate was stormed and saved by a single guard. No document of the Jaipur state names a gatekeeper called Ram Singh or describes his death. The tale of the royal family escaping through secret passages belongs to the same body of local legend as the stories of the tunnel between Amber and Jaigarh. The story of Ram Singh is best understood not as the record of one night, but as the garrison's own epic: a tale told to soldiers about what a soldier should be.

That is why, in the legend, his story is told to every new guard who comes to the fort. Old soldiers, the storytellers say, would take the young recruits up to the gate on their first night of duty and tell them of Ram Singh. They would point to the place where he stood and say: "He did not leave. Neither will you." Whether or not this custom was ever real, the story it describes is exactly the kind of tale that armies everywhere have used to teach loyalty and courage.

And then there is the ghost.

Since that night, the people of Amer say, Ram Singh has never stopped guarding Jaigarh. Watchmen on the ramparts, especially on nights without a moon, have spoken of a tall figure walking slowly along the walls in the old armour of a Rajput soldier, a long sword at his side, a turban on his head. He walks the same route every time, from the gate along the battlements and back again, as a sentry walks his round. If anyone calls out to him, he does not answer. If anyone follows him, he turns a corner of the wall and is gone.

Others say they have heard him rather than seen him: the slow tread of footsteps on the stone paths when no one is there, the faint clink of metal on metal, the sound of a heavy bar being tested on a gate that has long stood open. Some visitors say they have felt, standing near the old gate at dusk, that they were being watched, not unkindly, but closely, as a guard watches anyone who comes near his post.

None of these accounts has ever been confirmed, and the people who tell them often admit that the wind on the ridge plays tricks, that the old stones make strange sounds as they cool after a hot day, and that the imagination works hard in a dark and lonely place. But the tellers also say they would not want the stories to stop. To them, the phantom guard is not a frightening ghost. He is a protector.

In the legend, the people of the area honour him still. It is said that each year a small rite is performed in his memory, with a lamp lit and flowers offered near the gate, in the way that villages across Rajasthan honour the memory of warriors who died defending their homes. Whether such a rite is held at the fort today, and by whom, the accounts do not agree. But the spirit of the custom is old and real: across Rajasthan, memorial stones of fallen warriors, the *jhunjhar* and the hero-stones, stand at village edges and are given offerings, because the people remember those who died so that others might live.

So, when the sun goes down over the Hill of Eagles and the last visitors walk down the road to Amer, the walls of Jaigarh are left to the wind, the stars and, if the people of Amer are right, to one man who will not leave. Somewhere along the battlements, they say, Ram Singh is walking his round, as he has every night for more than two hundred years, keeping a gate that no one will ever storm again.

## Remembered for

- **The guardian fort.** Jaigarh, completed by Sawai Jai Singh II around 1726, was the arsenal and citadel above Amber and was never captured in war.
- **A troubled century.** The tale is set in the eighteenth century, when succession wars and Maratha demands threatened the Jaipur state.
- **The stand at the gate.** Legend tells of Ram Singh, a gatekeeper who refused an order to surrender and held the gate alone through the night. No record names him or describes such an assault.
- **Death at his post.** In the tale he was found dead at dawn with his sword raised and buried with honours near the gate.
- **The phantom on the ramparts.** Guards and visitors tell of a tall figure in Rajput armour walking the walls on moonless nights. These are stories, not evidence.
- **A lesson in loyalty.** The legend became the garrison's own epic, told to new guards as an example of duty, in the tradition of Rajasthan's hero-stones.

stories.title: The Underground Passage Network
stories.story:
## The Underground Passage Network — the hidden roads beneath the Aravallis

*The fortified passage between Amber and Jaigarh and the great water tanks beneath the fort are real and can be seen today; the fifteen-kilometre subterranean city, the hidden river, the murdered workers and the map divided among three ministers belong to the stories of guides and villagers. Where history and legend part ways, this story says so.*

Stand on the ramparts of **Jaigarh** at dusk and look down. Below you, on the slope of the same ridge, lies the palace of **Amber**, its pale walls turning amber and rose as the light goes. Below the palace lies **Maota Lake**, and around it the old town, and beyond that the long valley that leads south towards Jaipur. Between the summit and the palace there seems to be nothing but rock, scrub and the zigzag of the walls that climb the hill. But the people of Amer have always said that the hill is hollow, and that beneath your feet run roads that no enemy ever saw.

The truth begins with a simple military problem. Amber had been the capital of the **Kachwaha** Rajputs since the eleventh and twelfth centuries, and the palace that stands there now was largely built from the late sixteenth century onwards, under **Raja Man Singh I** and his successors. It was a palace made for display as much as for defence: courtyards, mirrored halls, gardens and terraces facing the lake. Above it, on the summit called the **Cheel ka Teela**, the Hill of Eagles, stood the fortifications that protected it. These were strengthened over generations and given much of their present form by **Sawai Jai Singh II**, who completed the great fort of Jaigarh around **1726**. If an enemy ever broke into the town below, the royal household needed a way to climb from the palace to the fort without crossing open ground under fire.

So a way was made. A **fortified passage** connects the palace of Amber to Jaigarh above it, climbing the ridge partly underground and partly between high protecting walls. Part of it has been restored and opened to visitors in recent years, and those who walk it today feel the old purpose in its stone: a narrow, steady path, shielded on both sides, built so that the king, his family and his treasure could pass from the palace to the citadel unseen. This was not unusual. Many Rajput forts had such routes, hidden stairs, covered ways and postern gates, because every ruler knew that a fortress is only as strong as its last line of retreat.

The second real wonder lies inside Jaigarh itself. Water was the great weakness of every hill fort in Rajasthan, where the rains come for a few weeks and then vanish for the rest of the year. Jaigarh solved this with a system of channels that gathered rainwater from the slopes of the hills and led it down into enormous **underground tanks** beneath the fort's courtyards. These cisterns are vast, dark chambers with vaulted roofs, cool even in the heat of June, built to keep a garrison alive through the longest siege. To a soldier lowering a bucket into the blackness, or a villager who heard of them only by rumour, they must have seemed like halls of a hidden world.

From these two real things, the passage and the tanks, the people of Amer built a legend.

The old men tell it slowly, the way such things are told. They say that the passage visitors walk today is only the smallest part of what lies beneath the hills. When the Kachwaha kings built their fort, they say, they did not stop at one tunnel. They dug and kept digging, for fifty years and more, until the whole ridge was threaded with roads. One road ran from Jaigarh to Amber. Another ran to **Nahargarh**, the fort on the hill above Jaipur. Others ran out into the folds of the Aravallis to hidden gates in lonely valleys, so that the royal family could slip out of a besieged fort and appear miles away, among friends, before the enemy knew they had gone. In the telling, the network stretched for **fifteen kilometres** or more.

The passages in the legend are not narrow. They are wide enough for horses to walk two abreast and for small carts to roll between the walls. Along them, the storytellers say, were chambers cut into the rock: storerooms heaped with grain and oil, armouries, rooms where soldiers slept, even small shrines where lamps burned before the images of the gods. In a long siege, they say, the royal family and their nobles could live beneath the hill for months in comfort, while the enemy above wondered why the defenders never seemed to grow hungry.

"But how did they breathe down there?" a child will ask, and the teller is ready. There were shafts, he says, cut up through the rock to the surface and hidden among boulders and thorn bushes, so that air came down but no one above could see where. There were lamps set in niches, and in some places light was brought down through narrow slits in the rock so cleverly that from the hillside they looked like nothing at all. And there was water. Far below the lowest passage, the legend says, ran a **secret underground river**, cold and sweet, that never dried even in years of famine.

Then the story turns darker, as such stories do. A work so great, the tellers say, could not be done by a few men. Thousands laboured on it, cutting the rock by hand and carrying the rubble out by night. And because the whole value of the network lay in its secrecy, the king could not allow those who knew it to go free. Here the voice drops. Many of the workers, the legend says, never came out. Some say they were walled up in the passages they had cut; others say they were simply never seen again. Their spirits, the old men add, still wander the dark galleries.

The builders, in the tale, were careful in other ways too. Some sections were made to collapse if an enemy found them: a pillar knocked away, a beam pulled, and the roof would come down and seal the passage forever. The network had several levels, one below another, so that an enemy who found one road would never guess at the road beneath it. And the full map was never written down in one place. It was divided, the story says, among **three trusted ministers**, each of whom knew only his own section. Only the king, if he called all three together, could follow the whole route from one end to the other.

None of this has been found. No survey of Jaigarh has revealed a fifteen-kilometre network of roads wide enough for carts, no subterranean river has been discovered beneath the fort, and no record of the court describes thousands of workers dying to keep a secret. A tunnel of the size the legend describes, running for miles through the hard rock of the Aravallis, would have been one of the greatest engineering works of its age, and it would have left traces in the account books, in the letters of the court, and in the memory of the many people who must have worked on it. Those traces are not there. The tale of the murdered workers, in particular, is a story that is told of many great buildings in India and around the world, from palaces to tombs, and it should be heard as a legend about the cruelty of power, not as an account of what happened at Jaigarh.

Yet it is easy to see why the legend grew. The real passage was hidden by design, and few ordinary people ever entered it. The real water tanks were enormous, and few ever saw inside them. Jaigarh itself was a closed fort for most of its history, a military place guarded by the state, where outsiders were not welcome. Rumours of treasure, which led to a real government search of the fort in **1976**, made people even more certain that there was more beneath the hill than anyone would admit. When a place is secret, people fill the silence with stories, and the stories always grow larger than the truth.

There is also a deeper reason. The Kachwahas had survived for centuries by being careful. They served the Mughal emperors and grew powerful in that service, but they knew how quickly favour could turn. Sawai Jai Singh II had lost his own capital to the emperor **Bahadur Shah** in 1707 and had won it back only with the help of his allies. In the decades after his death in 1743, armies crossed the Jaipur lands again and again, in the war between his sons **Ishwari Singh** and **Madho Singh** and in the Maratha campaigns that followed. A royal house that had lived through such times would indeed have planned its escape routes with care. The legend simply takes that real caution and multiplies it many times over.

Today the guides of Amer still tell the story, and they tell it well. As they lead visitors through the restored passage, they stop at a bend or a blocked opening in the wall. "This one," they say, "was sealed long ago. No one knows where it goes." Some speak of unexplored sections that still lie beyond the bricked-up arches, holding old weapons, pots, coins and, perhaps, the bones of those who lived and died in the dark. Visitors lean close to the cool stone and listen, half expecting to hear footsteps on the other side.

Perhaps there are a few forgotten stairs and storerooms still hidden in the old fort; many great forts keep small secrets that surveys have not yet reached. But the real marvel of Jaigarh's hidden ways is not a lost city beneath the hills. It is the skill of the builders who carried a safe road up a steep ridge, gathered the scarce rain of the desert into great dark tanks, and made a fort that could hold out long after the plains below had fallen. The legend of the underground network is the story people told to explain that skill, a story in which the hill above Amber became hollow, and every closed door led somewhere no one could follow.

## Remembered for

- **The fortified passage to Amber.** A real protected route, partly underground, connects the palace of Amber with Jaigarh above it; part of it is open to visitors today.
- **The great water tanks.** Vast underground cisterns fed by rain channels kept Jaigarh supplied through long sieges and inspired tales of hidden halls.
- **The legend of the hollow hill.** Local tradition tells of a fifteen-kilometre network of passages, chambers and shrines; no such network has been found.
- **The secret river and the three ministers.** Folklore speaks of an underground river and of a map divided among three trusted men, each knowing only his own section.
- **The tale of the lost workers.** The story that the builders were killed to keep the secret is a legend told of many great buildings, not a recorded event.
- **The caution of the Kachwahas.** The legend magnifies a real habit of a royal house that had learned through wars and sieges to plan its escape routes with care.

stories.title: The Foundry of Miracles
stories.story:
## The Foundry of Miracles — fire, bronze and legend on the Hill of Eagles

*The cannon foundry of Jaigarh and the great gun Jaivana cast there in 1720 are matters of history; the mantras that made metal unbreakable, the "Seven Thunders" with their impossible powers and the abandoned workshop found by the British belong to the stories told about the fort. Where history and legend part ways, this story says so.*

The fire was never allowed to die. That is how the old men of Amer begin the tale. Day and night, they say, through the cold winters and the furnace-heat of May, a red glow showed on the summit of the Hill of Eagles, and those who lived below could hear, carried down on the wind, the ringing of hammers and the roar of bellows. When strangers asked what was burning up there, the people of Amer would answer with a mixture of pride and fear: "That is the foundry of the king. They are making thunder."

The foundry was real. **Jaigarh**, the great fort that stands above the palace of **Amber**, was more than a garrison. It was the arsenal of the **Kachwaha** state, the place where its weapons were stored, repaired and made. Its walls enclosed workshops, storerooms and, most remarkable of all, a **cannon foundry**, one of the very few of its age in India that still survives with its furnace and working areas recognisable. The fort as it stands today owes most to **Sawai Jai Singh II**, who completed it around **1726**, and the foundry was one of the reasons he valued it so highly.

Jai Singh II was not an ordinary king. He was a soldier and a statesman who served the Mughal emperors as a high-ranking noble and governor, and who founded the new city of **Jaipur** in **1727**. But he was also a man of learning, fascinated by mathematics and astronomy. He built the great stone observatories called **Jantar Mantar** at Jaipur, Delhi and other cities, gathered scholars at his court, and took a keen interest in the knowledge of other lands, including the astronomical work of European Jesuits. A ruler with such a mind would naturally have cared about the science of metal and fire, and about the guns on which the safety of his state depended.

Gunfounding had come to India in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, carried by many hands: by Ottoman and Persian gunners who served Indian rulers, by the Portuguese on the western coast, and by the artillery masters of the Mughal armies. By the eighteenth century, Indian founders were casting guns of great size and beauty in bronze and in iron, and the courts of the Rajput states kept their own workshops. The foundry at Jaigarh belonged to this tradition. Its craftsmen melted metal in furnaces built into the hill, poured it into moulds set in a deep casting pit, and then bored and finished the barrels with heavy machinery. A great boring mechanism survives in the fort today, and visitors stand before it and try to imagine the power needed to turn it.

The greatest work of this foundry stands a short walk away. In **1720**, the founders of Jaigarh cast **Jaivana**, a cannon so enormous that it is often described as the largest cannon on wheels in the world. Its barrel is more than six metres long, and the whole gun weighs around fifty tonnes. It sits on a massive wheeled carriage beneath its own canopy, its barrel decorated with carved designs, pointed out over the hills towards the south. To make such a gun, the foundry had to melt and pour an enormous quantity of metal in a single casting, a task that demanded skill, organisation and a great deal of courage.

From these real achievements, the people of Amer built a legend of a foundry where miracles were made.

In the legend, the master craftsmen of Jaigarh had learned their secrets from wandering metal-workers who came from Persia and from the lands of the Europeans, men who had travelled through many kingdoms and knew the arts of many peoples. The old founders listened, learned, and then went further than their teachers. They developed, the story says, a secret way of purifying metal. As the ore and the bronze melted in the furnace, priests and craftsmen together chanted particular mantras, and the sound, the tellers insist, entered the metal and changed it.

What came out of that furnace, in the legend, was no ordinary metal. The cannons it made never needed cleaning; the soot of the powder slid off them like water off a lotus leaf. The swords never dulled, however many battles they fought. The armour turned aside every blade and every ball. The craftsmen who made these things were treated like princes, given fine houses and rich gifts, and bound by an oath of terrible strictness: whoever revealed the secrets of the foundry outside its walls would pay with his life.

The most famous products of the foundry, the tellers say, were seven great guns called the **"Seven Thunders"**. Each had its own power. One could be fired underwater. One could send its shot around the corner of a hill to strike an enemy who thought himself safe. One fired invisible balls that no one could see in flight, so that the enemy saw only their own walls falling. The other four, in the telling, had powers so strange that the storytellers argue about them to this day.

As the legend tells it, the foundry worked in shifts, team after team, so that the fire never cooled. One group tended the furnaces, another made the moulds, another poured, another bored and polished. The heat was controlled with perfect precision, the story says, by a system of underground furnaces and channels of water, so that the metal was never too hot or too cold.

Here history must speak plainly. There is no record of a cannon that fired underwater, around corners or with invisible shot; such guns are impossible, and they belong to the world of folk tales, like the flying carpets and magic swords of other storytellers. There is no evidence that mantras changed the nature of metal, though it is entirely possible that the founders, like craftsmen across India, prayed and performed rituals before a great casting, as an act of devotion and in hope of success. Every casting of a large gun was dangerous; a flaw in the mould or a crack in the metal could ruin months of work or kill the men around the pit, and it would have been natural for them to seek the blessing of the gods.

The legend also has a strange ending. When the British took control of Jaigarh, it says, they found the foundry abandoned but perfectly preserved, with tools and materials laid out as if the workers had only just stepped away. This part of the story cannot be true as it is told, because the British never took control of Jaigarh. In **1818** the state of Jaipur signed a treaty with the East India Company, accepting British protection and paramountcy, as many Rajput states did in those years. But its rulers kept their own forts, armies and administration, and Jaigarh remained in the hands of the Kachwaha house until after Indian independence, when Jaipur joined the new state of Rajasthan in **1949**. The foundry fell silent not because its workers vanished in a single night, but because the age of such great hand-cast guns slowly came to an end.

The legend says, too, that attempts to copy the methods of the old founders have failed, and that the craftsmen took their secrets to the grave. In a sense, there is truth in this. The skills of the traditional gunfounders were passed from master to apprentice by hand and by example, rarely written down, and when the work stopped, much of that knowledge was lost. It is not that their methods were magical. It is that they were human, carried in the hands and eyes of particular men, and when those men died, their knowledge died with them.

The story of Jaivana itself carries its own piece of legend. It is said that the great gun was fired only once, as a test, and that its ball flew so far that it landed near the town of **Chaksu**, some thirty-five kilometres away, where the impact made a hollow that filled with water and became a pond. Whether this firing really took place, and how far the ball truly travelled, cannot be confirmed. But the tale shows how deeply the people of the region were impressed by the power of the gun cast on their hill. Jaivana was never used in battle. It was a weapon of deterrence and of pride, a declaration that the state that owned it was strong.

Today the foundry is quiet. Visitors walk through the old workshop and look at the furnace, the casting pit and the heavy machinery, and then climb to the platform where Jaivana stands. Guides tell the stories of the Seven Thunders and the mantras, and many visitors listen with a smile. But when they stand beside the vast barrel of Jaivana, and imagine the molten metal that once ran glowing into its mould on this windy summit, they begin to understand why the people below believed that miracles were made here.

The true miracle of Jaigarh's foundry was not magic. It was the skill of the founders, who without modern machines melted, poured and shaped tonnes of metal into weapons of great power and beauty, working in heat and danger, on a hilltop far above the world. The legend of the Seven Thunders is what people made of that skill when they could not see it with their own eyes: a story in which fire and prayer and craft joined together to make thunder.

## Remembered for

- **A real cannon foundry.** Jaigarh's foundry is one of the very few of its age in India that still survives with its furnace, casting pit and machinery recognisable.
- **Jaivana (1720).** The giant cannon cast at Jaigarh, often called the largest cannon on wheels in the world, was never used in battle.
- **The legend of the mantras.** Folklore says chants spoken over the molten metal made cannons, swords and armour that never failed; this is legend, though the founders may well have prayed before great castings.
- **The Seven Thunders.** Tales of guns that fired underwater, around corners or with invisible shot belong to folklore, not history.
- **A corrected history.** The British never took control of Jaigarh; Jaipur accepted British protection by treaty in 1818 and kept its own forts until it joined Rajasthan in 1949.
- **The lost craft.** The skills of the old gunfounders, passed by hand from master to apprentice, faded when the work came to an end.
